# Preface

Reader, you who strictly follow your duties toward God, toward the state, toward your neighbor, and toward yourself, solely because Christianity commands you to do so: I beg you, set this book aside at first glance. Do not say: "Ha! You only make me curious; I must read it!" Believe me, you will lose your peace of mind <note>The original term *Seelenruhe* refers to a state of spiritual tranquility or inner peace, which the author suggests his radical critique might disrupt.</note> over it, and I then wash my hands in innocence <note>A biblical allusion to Pontius Pilate (Matthew 27:24), meaning the author takes no responsibility for the reader's potential distress.</note> because I told you beforehand. If you still will not take my advice, then read the Appendix as well, and read it again. Study it, and grasp it completely, if you have the strength for it. In doing so, you will find your peace of mind again, and you will fulfill all duties toward God, toward the state, toward your neighbor, and toward yourself with double the joy.

I divide the thinking-reading public, in regard to my book, into three classes. To the first, I count those who search for truth with an unbiased mind and accept it, whether it has been long recognized or only recently found: I say, to this class I count all those who set themselves above the prejudice that opinions and

IV

->**Preface**<-

doctrines should be true merely because they have been regarded as established truths by many for millennia. To the second [class], I count those who praise Voltaire <note>François-Marie Arouet (1694–1778), the famous French Enlightenment philosopher known for his wit and attacks on the established Catholic Church.</note> and his ilk as true lights of the world, and merely laugh at things they do not understand; who consider the doctrine of rewards and punishments beyond the grave to be an absurdity, and do not hesitate to become rogues as often as opportunities present themselves, as long as the authorities with their laws cannot get at them. To the third, finally, I count those who teach the people and have taken an oath of office that they will always present the opinions of the Church Fathers <note>The influential theologians of the early Christian Church whose writings established early orthodoxy.</note> as divine truths, even if they should immediately doubt one or the other.

My book cannot harm readers of the first class; it must rather benefit them, because they will grant me that I have sought the truth. In the traditional systems of folk religions <note>original: *Volksreligionen*; established, state-sanctioned religions practiced by the general populace.</note>, they find various dogmas that not only contradict reason but also frequently contradict each other. God is, as almost every religion teaches, most perfect in all his attributes. But no suffering belongs to the highest perfection. Nevertheless, God is said to have assumed a human body and suffered on earth for humanity, merely to satisfy his own justice.

<meta>catchword: Now</meta>

<column-break/>

V

->**Preface.**<-

Now, however, there are infinitely many globes <note>original: *Erdkugeln*; here the author references the "plurality of worlds," a popular 18th-century scientific and philosophical theory that other planets are inhabited.</note>, on all of which surely dwell human-like creatures who, without doubt, are just like us—not entirely perfect, not entirely without sin—because otherwise they would have to be equal to God, that is, be God himself in the proper sense. But should God go from one world, from one globe to another, to redeem all humans from the punishments of hell through his suffering, through his physical death? Then his existence would consist in a constant humiliation, in a constant suffering and dying for his creatures, who by their nature cannot possibly be perfect, cannot possibly be equal to him? But how can God demand the highest perfection from his creatures when he has not given them the capacity to become perfect? Such and many other considerations present themselves to the truth-loving thinker. Then he concludes that neither the Bible nor the Apostles' Creed is the true word of God, but rather human ordinance <term>human ordinance: *Menschensaßung*; a law or tradition created by humans rather than dictated by God.</term>. Then he examines the prophetic passages of scripture that are interpreted as referring to the Messiah, and finds highly striking correspondences between these ancient prophecies and those events that occurred with Jesus. Now he asks: how then did the prophets know all this, if they did not know it from divine revelation? Would their writings then be the word of God after all? And now he concludes: God is either angry and vengeful, like a stubborn master who demands supernatural services from his subjects that they cannot possibly perform, and then tortures himself as punishment <note>A reference to the doctrine of the Atonement, where God the Son suffers to satisfy the Father's justice.</note> just to satisfy his own justice; or all our fundamental laws of thought, all our generally recognized truths, are mere phenomena, mere imaginings, mere nervous spasms—not fundamental laws of thought, not fundamental truths from which I can derive new truths. What then becomes of the endurance of my soul? Am I perhaps myself only a phenomenon? Thus he wavers anxiously over terrifying abysses of agonizing doubts about life and death to the left and to the right, like a reed bent now this way, now that by the wind, which threatens to break it at any moment. So too did I waver in mortal anxieties, and nothing could protect me from the fall but God, by means of my reason. At the very least, I believe I know for certain that I now stand firm. Should I still waver, still err, then I ask for kind and thorough instruction; for I seek only truth, because I cannot be happy without it.

certainly gotten to know them as well; but may God preserve me from such people if all Christians I know were like all the followers of Voltaire <note>original: *Voltairianer*; disciples of the French Enlightenment philosopher Voltaire, often associated with deism and sharp critiques of organized religion.</note> who have made themselves known to me! According to their principles, they must indeed be as I have found them to be, and I would be very pleased if some of them allowed themselves to be converted by my book.

To readers of the third class, this book can likewise do no harm. They have not, after all, renounced the use of their reason, but have merely solemnly sworn not to publicly teach anything that runs contrary to the prevailing religious opinions. However, my book even shows them the most compelling reasons why they should not declaim against the prevailing doctrines—much less attempt to make unauthorized alterations to them—even if they recognize much of it to be false. Generally, no single man may or can make alterations in religious matters: for he alone can easily err, and with his innovations do more harm than good, since they affect the whole of society; consequently, they damage the whole too much if they do harm. Perhaps only the wisest of entire nations taken together, not individually, can gradually and successfully make alterations to old, harmful customs which are nonetheless held as sacred by the people. Without so-called revealed religion, the person who does not think for himself cannot exist <note>original: *bestehen*; here meaning to maintain one's moral or social standing/existence.</note>

IX

->**Preface**<-

at his best, and he cannot easily exchange his mysterious little verses—which he learns by heart as a boy without understanding anything of them—for others in old age that he is expected to learn anew and perhaps also does not understand. Rational school instruction in the lower classes, and in small towns or in the villages, will therefore likely remain the best means for the education of rational-thinking, good people. Thus, even teachers of the people <note>original: *Volkslehrer*; a term often used for local pastors and schoolmasters responsible for the moral education of the public.</note> can read my book without hesitation. If they seek truth and use their reason for good, then they, like men who look to the welfare of the whole, will know how to use the truth with wisdom. But if they do not seek truth, if they have renounced the use of their reason and consider rational doubt to be a sin, then my book cannot harm them anyway, because it contains nothing but rational reasonings, which they would simply reject.

Now, there is still something to be said about the various essays that appear in this book itself.

It is well known that many passages of the Bible, but especially the imagery of the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>, darken the minds of many people and even give rise to crimes. Rosenfeld <note>Johann Friedrich Rosenfeld, a 18th-century German radical who claimed to be the Messiah and led a small, controversial sect.</note> and his followers prove the legitimacy of their crimes from the Prophets and from the Revelation of John.

The Moravian "reborn" shepherd, who did not believe he was perfectly reborn or perfectly faithful if he could not sacrifice his most beloved as Abraham did, prayed to God for this cruel faith for so long until he felt faithful enough to strike his three boys dead with a wood-ax and offer them to God as a sacrifice, as a seal of his faith; as one reads in the first volume of the *Yearbooks of Taste and Enlightenment*. When the malcontents in the United Netherlands <note>Referring to the political turmoil in the Dutch Republic during the 1780s.</note> wish to insult the Hereditary Stadtholder now, they make use of biblical prophecies and call him the Antichrist—whether in jest or in earnest, I do not know. Should one therefore not be permitted to say how those ancient prophetic myths arose, and how they attained the dignity of divine truths?

On page 78, I asked doubtfully whether perhaps the four World Ages of the ancients did not arise merely from the precession of the equinoxes, but also from the four seasons? # Preface

XII

->**Preface**<-

...Platonic years <note>A "Platonic Year" or "Great Year" refers to the time it takes for the constellations to complete a full cycle of the precession of the equinoxes, approximately 25,800 years.</note> sufficiently. Poets, who made use of the four ages of the world and employed those derived from the precession of the equinoxes, began with the golden age, followed by the silver, then the bronze, and finally the iron. This was because the Lion <note>the constellation Leo</note> appeared yellow or golden; the Bull <note>Taurus</note>—specifically that white bull into which Jupiter was said to have once transformed, and which appears with a solemn, beautiful whiteness in the heavens—appeared white or silver; the ancient Egyptian water-bucket or Canobus <note>Referring to the constellation Aquarius, sometimes associated with the Egyptian deity Canopus or a water jar.</note>, that is, the Water-bearer, appeared bronze; and finally the Scorpion <note>Scorpio</note> appeared black or iron. Others, however, who created their four world-ages from the four seasons, placed the silver first, then the golden, followed by the iron, and finally the bronze. They did this because they began counting with spring (the white Bull), then named the summer (the yellow Lion), then proceeded to autumn (the black, iron Scorpion), and ended with winter (the bronze Water-bucket). Therefore, the first rider in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation, chapter 6.</note> can quite rightly ride a white horse, the second a red horse, the third a black horse, and the fourth a pale horse. "A measure of wheat for a denarius, three measures of barley for a denarius; and do not harm the oil and the wine" <note>A quotation from Revelation 6:6 regarding the third horseman.</note> thus fits perfectly with the fruit-heavy autumn and the just distribution of the provisions that the autumn provides in the land where the zodiac

You will also not be mistaken if you derive the Angel Gabriel, who likewise appears often in this book, from Mercury <note>The Roman messenger god, known as Hermes in Greek.</note>, or associate him with him.

Regarding the prophecies of the Messiah, I have not been permitted to involve myself in philological investigations because my book is intended to be a reader, not a reference book for exegetes <note>Scholars who provide critical interpretations of scripture.</note>. If, however, it is believed that my explanations do not correspond to the meaning of the text, I am willing to write a commentary on the matter to show clearly that the entire language of the prophets is exactly the language of the ancient astrologers, and owes its origin solely to the observers of the heavens. I will then clearly demonstrate that all folk religions flow fundamentally from a common source: the ancient observations of celestial and natural events. Heaven and nature are those great books in which all nations, as culture began to awaken, have read—and still read—almost entirely the same events from the beginning. # Preface

XIV

->**Preface**<-

...garments. Truly, the arrogant priests <note>original: "Sacerdoten"</note> of one nation or another dressed those ancient observations of the heavens and nature in various dark veils, so that the uninitiated <note>original: "Profanen"</note>, who did not belong to their learned tribes, could not find the key to their secret science. But it also happened that, eventually, the husks themselves were mistaken for the seeds, the poems for truths, the shadow for the essence, and the figurative representations of celestial and natural events for divine revelations. Men cut up the mantle of truth to make a new one out of it, and they believed they had created a new truth themselves, although it remained hidden, unnoticed beneath the shredded mantle. They turned the mantle inside out; yet they still did not recognize the truth that had been lost within it. Generally, they looked only at the mantle and not at the truth itself. Jews, Christians, Turks <note>A common historical term for Muslims in 18th-century European writing.</note>, and all heathens fundamentally have only one single religion, regardless of how differently their mythologies turn out, and regardless of the fact that they believe they have very different religions. These supposedly different religions have all flowed from the great book of the heavens, from the Book of Nature. They all unite in celestial and natural events, like many spread-out threads that run together into a common knot.

<meta>catchword: From</meta>

<column-break/>

XV

->**Preface**<-

Regarding the contemplation of Jesus and his disciples, there is nothing further to report than that I am ready to publicly recant as soon as I am thoroughly refuted. Perhaps some of my readers will even reproach me for not declaring the accounts of Jesus found in the so-called Evangelists to be lies—which were allegedly forged long after his lifetime—but I preferred to give these writings too much credit rather than too little. Furthermore, anyone who is unwilling to accept my explanation of that miraculous calming of the stormy sea might simply assume that the storm subsided of its own accord due to ordinary causes just as Jesus commanded it to be still. However, if one objects to my explanation of the resurrection story by saying that Jesus, on account of his foot wounds, could by no means have walked to Bethany and to Emmaus <note>The text spells this "Emabus," likely an archaic variant or printing error for the biblical town of Emmaus.</note> if he had been a mere human, then one must first prove to me that he was actually nailed through the feet, and not merely tied, before I can grant this objection any weight.

As for the Appendix, I hope it will make amends for what the book perhaps seems to make worse. Had I not been able to show my readers a new harbor for their peace of mind, I would never have dared to show them the shallowness...

<page-num>XVI</page-num>
<header>Preface</header>

...obsoleteness and the silting up <note>original: "Versandung," a metaphor for how the original meaning of ancient traditions has become buried or clogged over time, like a waterway.</note> of the old; for one must take nothing from the public if one cannot give them something better in its place. All religions have arisen from the contemplation of nature, especially the heavens: therefore I too, quite naturally, have derived my religious principles from the contemplation of nature. In ancient times, because of a lack of instruments, one could not arrive at any complete or true knowledge of nature, and what was known was presented under the veil of hieroglyphs <note>In the 18th century, "hieroglyphs" often referred generally to any symbolic or coded communication, not just Egyptian writing.</note> or in mystical expressions. From this arose mysterious religions; from this arose religions that appeared to be very different from one another. At present, there prevails in astronomy and natural science at least clarity and agreement: therefore, clarity and agreement must also prevail in the religious propositions that flow from them.

I have called my book *Astrognostic Final Judgment* <note>original: "Astrognostisches Endurtheil"</note> because <term>Astrognosy: The study of the fixed stars and constellations, focusing on their positions and names as seen by the naked eye, rather than their physical or mathematical properties.</term> is the knowledge of the apparent position and the apparent course of the stars, but does not, like astronomy, concern itself with mathematical measurements of the true motion, the true size, and the true distance of the stars from one another. Among the ancients, astronomy was almost nothing more than mere astrognosy. This they combined with astrology, or with that deceptive art of [predicting] from the constella-

<meta>catchword: stella-</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>XVII</page-num>
<header>Preface</header>

-tions. From these two arts, from astrognosy and astrology, they forged their prophecies and their religious systems.

I call the movement of the equinoxes <note>original: "Nachtgleichpunkte," literally "night-equal points."</note> *precession* <term>Precession: The slow change in the orientation of Earth's rotational axis, which makes the stars appear to shift positions over thousands of years.</term> because I look mainly at the constellations which, according to the order of the signs, move away from the imagined points. If one looks at the points themselves, one must say *recession* or regression instead of precession, as is clear in itself.

Gold and silver must never fall below the value determined by the needs of the miners, the smelters, and the owners of the mines who consume resources while these metals are being extracted, refined, or minted. But if they are produced without special effort and without cost, their value falls lower, and thus the state is defrauded. There is no shortage of these metals in the world; consequently, one does not perform any act of charity for the world by making them. No private individual should ever bring gold and silver into public circulation, for this business belongs solely to the state or its sovereign.

# Introduction.

When all patriarchs <note>The German *Hausväter* refers to the heads of households or "house-fathers," often used in a biblical or pastoral sense to describe the leaders of self-sufficient family units.</note> were still farmers and shepherds, and all farmers and shepherds were yet kings who lived together with their livestock and their children and servants: in those early times, they knew no further measure of time than the duration of the apparent daily revolution of the heavens, which we call the **natural day**. Every time the sun went down, they would place a stone in a specifically chosen location, and afterward, they would count the elapsed days by these gathered stones; for they could not properly record the number of days because they did not yet possess the art of writing.

However, as these stones accumulated immensely within a few generations and could no longer be conveniently counted, the observers of the heavens soon found themselves forced to seek a larger measure of time. They found it in the periodic change of the moonlight, and now likewise placed a stone in its place every time they observed this change. We call this measure—which actually consists of twenty-nine days along with several additional hours—<note>The text breaks off here; the next page likely continues with "and..." to complete the definition of a month.</note>

<note>Vocabulary: Introduction, Patriarchs/Heads of Household, Measure of time, Revolution of the heavens, Day, Moonlight, Chronology.</note>

<summary>The author describes the primitive origins of time-keeping, explaining how early nomadic leaders moved from counting individual days with stones to observing the lunar cycle as a more efficient system.</summary>
<keywords>astronomy, chronology, natural day, lunar cycle, history of writing, patriarchs, timekeeping</keywords>

--- Page 20 ---
<meta>Continuing from the previous page, the author finishes the definition of a lunar month as a unit of time derived from the physical phases of the moon.</meta>

<page-num>4</page-num>
<header>Introduction.</header>
<meta>catchword: well</meta>

and minutes contains a **month** <note>German: *Mond*, literally "moon," here referring to the lunar month</note>: but those earliest inventors of the same may have well estimated it at only twenty-eight days, regardless of the fact that long after them it was extended to thirty days by the **Chaldeans** <note>Ancient inhabitants of Mesopotamia, famed in the 18th century as the founding fathers of astronomy</note>.

From the alternation of the moonlight also arose the **week**, which likewise provided a convenient measure of time. When the moon is "new" today, after seven days it turns half of its illuminated side toward the earth, and is called the **first quarter**. After twice seven days, it turns its entire light side toward us and is called **full moon**. After three times seven days, we again see only half of its illuminated hemisphere and call it the **last quarter**. After four times seven days, we see nothing of it once more and call it the **new moon**. Nothing was therefore more natural and reasonable than for people to make this small period of seven days into a measure of time, especially since they could use it very conveniently to designate the elapsed quarters of the moon.

The **Mosaic creation story** <note>The account of the world's beginning in the biblical Book of Genesis</note> therefore has no part in the origin of the week, and can have none: for creation still continues uninterrupted even now, and will likely never be completed in all eternity. But of course, to realize this, one must be well-versed in modern **astronomy** <note>German: *Sternkunde*</note>, as well

<page-num>5</page-num>
<header>Introduction</header>
<sig>C 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: un-</meta>

well as in **natural history** <note>German: *Naturgeschichte*, the study of the physical world</note>.

Thereupon, those earliest observers of the heavens also perceived that the sun itself seemed to travel around the sky from west to east, albeit slowly but nonetheless regularly. Since they spent the greater part of their lives under the open sky, and consequently could observe the course of the stars at leisure: they gradually became aware that during each such revolution of the sun, exactly the same number of days, weeks, and months passed. They therefore also made this period of revolution into a measure of time—that is, they invented the **year**, and afterward likewise marked each one with a stone. At present, the duration of the year has certainly been precisely determined; but one must not seek such precision in high antiquity. It was initially estimated at only three hundred and fifty days, or at twelve twenty-nine-day months along with two **intercalary days** <note>German: *Schalttage*, extra days added to align the calendar with the solar year</note>: but later, when thirty days were reckoned to a month, it was given three hundred and sixty days.

In such a way, they gradually organized astrology into a system, which found all the more admiration and was regarded as all the more sacred, the greater the confusion, the more impenetrable the darkness, and the more artificial the ambiguities that prevailed within it.

Some of those who forged this system may well have known that it had no firm foundation: for otherwise they could have said everything clearly and would not have needed to wrap their prophecies in confused images or ambiguous speeches first. When they multiplied this number by the orbital period of one planet or another, it yielded a secondary period; at the conclusion of which, they claimed the same distress would return to the world. Thus, every tragic event gave rise to seven different periods, because they counted seven planets and assigned a specific nature to each. The happiness and pleasure of entire nations do not stand out as much as tribulation and general national distress: therefore, they rarely created periods of good significance. From this, it is sufficiently clear why most of these numbers are of a dreadful <note>German: "schauervoll" - evoking a sense of horror or religious awe</note> nature. In the same way, they created new prophetic numbers when it rained too much for several months, or when the lands where they resided were laid waste by pestilence, war, and locusts. In short, the obscurities and confusions that crept into this science due to the many absurd additions became immensely great.

The moon, on the other hand, left at least the stars of the first three magnitudes visible every night, especially when it appeared half-full or crescent-shaped. Thus, nothing was more natural than that the observers of its course and its changing light took particular notice of those stars at which it set heliacally <term>Heliacal setting: the last time a celestial body is visible in the morning twilight before it is lost in the sun's glare</term> each time—that is, where it hid itself beneath the sun’s rays on the morning horizon. 

The ancients always considered this heliacal setting to be the end of the old moon, just as they considered its heliacal rising, or its emergence from the sun's rays on the evening horizon, to be the beginning of the new one. Every time it set heliacally, they would, as mentioned, place a stone in a sacred place chosen for that purpose; and from this it is sufficiently clear why they observed this event so carefully, and why the constellation at which it appeared for the last time each month drew their entire attention.

<page-num>17</page-num>
# Introduction

Now, however, it does not always set heliacally at one and the same constellation: for each time it moves forward toward the east by roughly a twelfth part of the zodiac <term>Zodiac: the "circle of animals," the belt of the heavens through which the sun, moon, and planets appear to move</term>. For this reason, the ancients immediately organized the stars they found in these twelve locations of the sky into twelve special groups. For convenience in thought and speech, they visualized each group under an image that had some relation to the natural occurrences that took place at the end of each moon in their land and among their livestock.

Thus, the star group at which the moon set heliacally while the sheep were lambing was designated by a **Lamb**, which was later transformed into a **Ram** <note>original: "Widder"</note>. Four weeks later, it set heliacally again, and around this time most cows were calving: therefore, the star group at which it now disappeared was shaped like a **Calf**, or else like a young **Bull** <note>original: "Stier"</note>. Again, after approximately four weeks, the goats were giving birth: consequently, the constellation where the moon appeared for the last time in the morning twilight was given the form of two young **Goats**, which other peoples soon after transformed into the two twin brothers, **Castor** and **Pollux**. The following moon expired in the morning before the sun rose, as the sun had reached the northern tropic <note>The Tropic of Cancer, the northernmost point where the sun appears directly overhead</note> and now began to move back—

Above all others, the one we call the **Celestial Wagon** <note>original: "Himmelswagen"—the Big Dipper or Ursa Major</note> first drew the eyes of observers: for because of the seven bright stars shining within it, it is the most magnificent group of the northern sky, and at the latitude where those oldest astronomers lived, it never sets, but instead revolves there incessantly above the horizon around the pole. Through continued observation, humans further learned of the great influence of the sun's light on the creation and preservation of animals and plants. From the sun, they inferred the moon and believed that it likewise played a large part in the business of procreation and preservation, because it appeared to them as the most prominent celestial body after the sun. Therefore, they likely depicted these two "lights of the world" like husband and wife, who were engaged in the very act of procreation, and from whom the generated life of animals and plants emerged in a third form. Since the earliest humans, as stated, had not the slightest knowledge of the laws of motion nor of other principles of modern **natural science**, they could easily fall into the thought upon viewing the heavens that not only the planets but also the other stars were living beings. Thus, these images soon attained great dignity after their creation, because in the eyes of the learned and the ignorant masses alike, they now represented nothing less than deities. From this, one can easily perceive why the same images in different countries and among different nations—into whose hands they may have come partly through war and partly through migration—have given rise to entirely different concepts, and why the mythology of the Greeks is constituted so differently from that of the Egyptians, Chaldeans, Phoenicians, Hebrews, Chinese, Brahmins, Jews, and Christians.

Zoroaster <note>original: "Zorste," an archaic/shortened form of the name of the Persian prophet.</note> is said to have introduced the mysteries there, and to have given his initiates Mithra <note>The ancient Persian deity of light and covenants.</note>—the pure eternal light or the fire of the sun—as the supreme god, while subordinating the other celestial bodies to him as mere demons: and it is known that the worship of fire has continuously survived in many places in the Orient.

From the mysteries of Isis <note>The Egyptian goddess whose cult was famous for its secret initiation rites.</note>, the mysteries of Ceres <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Demeter; her mysteries at Eleusis were the most famous of the ancient world.</note> were formed, which later came to Athens. Thus, it is not even necessary to claim that all similar ideas among unlike and widely separated nations must necessarily have come from a single ancestral tribe. The similarity of such concepts is written so clearly in the heavens and in nature itself that they must have been easily recognized, at least across the entire northern temperate zone of the earth.

# First Vision

regarded his crucified Master. — Now, however, I will explain what it actually represents.

It is well known that the ancient Egyptians, and Moses as their pupil, believed—according to their creation story—that the globe of the Earth was created first, and shortly thereafter the sun, moon, and all other stars were formed from it. This was believed even though the sun is many millions of years older than the Earth, and although the upper planets, **Coelus** <note>The Latin name for the sky god, later used for the planet Uranus</note> or **Cybele** <note>An ancient Phrygian earth goddess; her use here as a planetary name reflects archaic or speculative astronomical naming</note>, **Saturn**, **Jupiter**, and **Mars**, were cast out from the sun much earlier, while the lower planets, **Venus** and **Mercury**, were cast out much later than the Earth and its moon—much like pumice and slag are ejected from raging volcanoes. This is something that all those who have familiarized themselves with mathematics and physics will easily admit. Furthermore, it is known that the earliest geographers knew only Asia and Africa, and perhaps not even those two continents in their entirety; consequently, they only knew of the three northern climate zones, as they believed the Earth rested upon golden mountains beyond the torrid zone. I also hardly need to mention that in ancient times, the seven <term>geniuses</term> <note>guiding spirits or tutelary deities believed to govern the motions and influence of celestial bodies</note>—who, according to the teachings and customs of the time, carried the seven planets around the heavens—were turned into the seven most noble spirits, or archangels, who stood before the Lord to carry out his commands; that is, those who constantly flew around the Earth,

<column-break/>

## Revelation I. 10 — 18.

and directed not only all natural events but also the destinies of mankind.

The green, turquoise-colored man discussed here thus signified the Earth, which then, just as now, had a green appearance in most regions due to the green herbs and trees. The light garment surrounding him indicated the clouds or the atmosphere; and his glowing thighs had to represent the golden mountains upon which the Earth was believed to rest at that time. The golden belt around the loins represented the torrid zone <note>the tropics</note>, where the sun’s rays formerly set almost everything ablaze. His rear countenance was the temperate zone, or the serene climate of the ancient stargazers who first painted this image; meanwhile, his snow-white hair signified the highest northern regions, where snow remains throughout summer and winter. The seven stars he held in his hand were the seven planets, which were always linked to the Earth, just as the seven lampstands—which were sometimes also painted as seven burning torches—indicated nothing more than the seven geniuses by whom the planets were carried around the heavens and all events on Earth were orchestrated. But I cannot believe that a sword proceeded from his mouth; rather, only a broad beam emerged, which was similar to a gust of wind <note>original: "Windstrahle"</note>,

Outside of the Zodiac, the Chaldeans and Persians, as **Diodorus Siculus** <note>original: "Diodor von Sicilien"; a Greek historian of the 1st century BC.</note> reports, counted twenty-four more constellations in the heavens. Twelve of these, which according to their lore never set but stood constantly in the northern sky above the horizon, were then the masters and rulers of the day, or of the living. The remaining twelve, on the other hand, which were located in the southern hemisphere of the sky below the horizon and never rose but remained constantly invisible, had command only over the night and over the dead. But all twenty-four taken together were the judges of all men, the dead and the living, and were likewise placed around the Earth. Finally, they also drew the heavens themselves in the form of a blue circular wall around the entire painting. Thus, the images of this supposed second vision were nothing more than the astrological symbols of the heavens and the terrestrial globe, and in regard to the future they signify likewise — nothing.

The green man, who sat upon the throne and had a rainbow around his head, was therefore once again the old symbol of the Earth; but here it stood in the middle of the hollow celestial sphere, and consequently gave our author—or at least the older prophets from whom he presumably borrowed the whole fable—the occasion to now place the scene of the apparition in heaven. ...of the most beautiful jasper and sardonyx." <note>This completes the sentence from the previous page describing the appearance of the figure on the throne.</note> For no rainbow is merely green; rather, it is red, yellow, green, blue, and violet. The four beasts, however, which stood around the Man and around the throne, were the four constellations of the <term>Zodiac<gloss>The belt of the heavens; here specifically the "Fixed Cross" of signs.</gloss></term>: the Lion, the Bull, the Aquarius, and the Scorpio. The latter was regarded by non-astronomical stargazers as a flying eagle because of its outstretched claws and many feet; in their opinion, such an evil creature as the scorpion could by no means have entered heaven. They also did not have six wings, but only four, and two hands each, which the author <note>Referring to the author of the Book of Revelation.</note> mistook for wings. The four wings indicated that their flight was directed toward all four quarters of the world. The two hands, on the other hand, signify nothing more than the help they provided to mankind, according to the delusions of the ancients. They were also "full of eyes" inside and out, which means they were covered everywhere with stars, because the figures themselves consist of nothing but stars. They could not rest—

The twenty-four elders, who sat in a wide circle around the seat of the Earth and were clothed in white garments, represented the aforementioned twenty-four constellations. Black and colorful clothes would certainly not have suited these figures, which were supposed to consist of nothing but stars and thus necessarily had to be enveloped in white light.

From the reversed order in which the author named the **four beasts**, it is clearly evident that either he, or his teacher, must have been accustomed to reading not like the Hebrews from right to left, but like the Greeks from left to right. Therefore, in order to leave a record for their descendants of this atmospheric phenomenon—which was perhaps rare to them—they first marked the four regions of the world on a tablet, and then added a large fiery cloud that came up from the north. In the middle of this cloud, they left a clear white space to indicate the bright spots where the stars appeared. But in the Southeast and West of the tablet, they painted a wide, sprawling sea, which represented the part of the sky left clear by the Northern Lights. Finally, to indicate the rain that followed this phenomenon, they placed the sun in the highest part of the heavens in the form of a man on a blue chair, and let rays emanate from him, which descended into the clouds and formed all the colors of the rainbow.

Long afterward, an astronomer who is said to have been named Atlas invented the armillary sphere <term>armillary sphere: a model of the celestial globe consisting of a spherical framework of rings, known in the text as a Ringsphäre</term> of the heavens, which, as is well known, consisted of four equally large rings nested within one another. Two of them formed the four colures <term>colures: the two principal meridians of the celestial sphere that intersect at the poles</term>, one the equator, and

<column-break/>

<page-num>73</page-num>
<header>Revelation 4:1–8</header>

and one the ecliptic <note>original: *Sonnenbahn* or "sun-path"</note>, on which the twelve constellations of the zodiac, or at least the four beasts of the solstices and equinoxes, were indicated. The rings were painted green or blue and adorned with stars because they represented the heavens, which shine everywhere with stars.

All these images and inventions later came to the keepers of the ancient mysteries, to the priests and stargazers of that time in Babylon, Memphis, Thebes, and so forth. Perhaps out of jealousy, or perhaps often out of ignorance, they did not explain the true meaning and use of these things to any profane person <note>In this context, "profane" refers to the uninitiated or common people outside the priestly class.</note>, but instead gave it to be understood that the great secrets of the gods—indeed, the future destinies of the world itself and of all mankind—lay hidden within them. Ezekiel, too, believed this; he probably had been able to catch nothing more of their hieroglyphs than the aforementioned images, which he now combined and presented as images of the glory of God that had appeared to him. He did this to give himself the reputation of a great prophet among his superstitious nation, which at that time imagined itself to be almost more than a king.

Thus, that fiery cloud coming from the north was nothing more than an Aurora Borealis <note>original: *Nordlicht*</note>, and those four beasts that appeared within it were nothing more than the four beasts

painted as a coiled snake, which ate its own tail in its gullet, and thus seemed to have neither beginning nor end. <note>The author is describing the Ouroboros, an ancient symbol of eternity and cyclicality.</note> Now, however, this symbol did not suit the fleeting nature of time, which they also found necessary to represent in many cases. They therefore had to create a new one, and for this they chose a swift animal, a horse. To give it even more speed, they added a pair of wings to its shoulder blades, and they painted only the front part of it, thereby indicating that only one part of time had fleetingly passed, while the other was still in the future.

The ancient Egyptians used this image to indicate the fleeting nature of the nine **monads** <note>German: *Monaden*. Here, the author likely refers to "monads" as fundamental units of time or the nine working months of the Egyptian calendar.</note> of their fieldwork. Namely, instead of a calendar, they placed a symbol in a public place every moon, which indicated the tasks that fell within that very moon. To this, they probably also added the winged horse each time, seeking thereby to encourage the people to be diligent.

But the Greeks transformed these symbols of the new working months into nine industrious maidens, the nine Muses; the aforementioned symbol of fleetingness, however, they turned into the horse of the Muses <note>Referring to Pegasus, the winged horse of Greek mythology.</note>; and finally, the symbols of the remaining three moons—during which the Egyptians, because of the overflow-

<meta>catchword: ing</meta>

Thus, the four horses in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> are likely nothing more than the symbols of four different periods of time. That the division of the zodiac into twelve constellations was one of the first labors of the ancient stargazers—and that the number of these images did not arise by chance, but was made neither larger nor smaller because the moon sets heliacally <term>heliacal: the last visible setting of a star or planet in the evening twilight before it is lost in the sun's glare</term> twelve times a year near twelve different groups of stars—was likewise shown in detail in the introduction. In the same way, I also proved there that those ancient stargazers, to whom these oldest astronomical works are attributed, lived at a considerable latitude within our temperate zone of the earth.

According to this arrangement, the names of the days followed one another in this fashion: **Saturn-day** <note>Saturday</note>, **Sunday**, **Monday**, **Mars-day** <note>Tuesday</note>, **Venus-day** <note>Friday</note>, **Jove-day** <note>Thursday</note>, and **Mercury-day** <note>Wednesday</note>.

From the cited order of the planets, one sees that the oldest astronomers in East India and Babylon estimated the distance of **Mercury** from the Earth to be greater than the distance of **Venus**; but the Egyptians reversed the matter and placed **Venus** further away from us than **Mercury**. Both parties were sometimes right and sometimes wrong in this, and could consequently very well waver back and forth between this or that opinion: for **Venus** is, as is well known, often actually much closer to us than **Mercury**, just as the latter is often much closer to us than **Venus**. One would think this minor astronomical dispute could have changed nothing in the world, since today much greater differences among the learned change nothing in the world. However, it changed a great deal: it placed the

# Second Continuation of the Second Vision

Herein lies the reason why only four horses with their riders appeared to the author of the Apocalypse under the **first four seals**, which he saw broken by the **Ram** <note>original: *Widder*; referring to the constellation Aries</note>, or according to his interpretation, by the **Lamb**, and why entirely new vistas presented themselves to him upon the breaking of the last three seals. He had, namely, the firm intention to perceive within those seven seals the seven ages of the **world**, and to see within the images—which he claimed to have seen after the breaking of these seals—all events, those already past as well as those yet to come. He also knew that those **four** images of the first four world ages were already a few millennia old. Consequently, according to his chronology, the sixth world age necessarily had to be coming to an end even then; the great Sabbath of the Lord had to be already dawning. 

To this were added the loathsome heathens, the Romans, who at that time had just resolved to put an end to his nation. Out of that Jewish vain pride, he regarded his nation as the most distinguished, the first, the oldest nation in the world, the only people of the Most High. Thus, for this reason, he was firmly convinced in his mind that with his nation every other kingdom on earth must simultaneously cease, the sixth world age must end, the great Sabbath of the Lord must begin, and the Messiah must now come for the second time—especially since the Messiah seemed to have promised to rebuild the temple, to

Morality such as this can hardly be found among entirely raw, uncivilized people, let alone among the chosen.

Now, at last, the **sixth world age** under the **sixth seal** comes to light, with which the reigns of the six lower planets end. The sun becomes black as a sackcloth of hair, and the moon becomes red as blood.

We must admit that both of these phenomena have indeed occurred often: for who does not know that the sun appears black during solar eclipses, while the moon appears red during total lunar eclipses? But against the author's childish concept of the **stars**, which he has falling to the earth like ripe figs from a fig tree, and against that simple fairy tale that represents the **heaven** as a hollow ceiling that is supposed to roll up and vanish like a strip of parchment—whereupon the powerful, the rich, the servants, the free, in short, all people, naturally crawl into rocky clefts in terror—I have nothing at all to say. The great ignorance of the ancient astrologers and of our author shines through all too clearly, and therefore allows for no serious refutation.

The **four corners of the earth** signify the **four cardinal directions**: for the earth is a spheroid and does not actually have four corners. But the **four angels** whom the author saw standing at these four corners of the world were the four ancient images of the **gods of the wind**. According to the delusions of many nations, these gods were sometimes depicted with puffed-out cheeks, blowing storms across the earth and sea from all four directions. Since winter and summer, frost and heat, thirst and hunger, thunder and storm-winds, toil and labor were meant to cease at the end of the **sixth world age**—according to Jewish fables—so that the **great Sabbath of the Lord** <note>The author uses "Sabbath" here to refer to a thousand-year period of rest or the "Millennium" expected after 6,000 years of history.</note> could begin: thus the storm-winds were no longer permitted to damage the seas, lands, or trees, but had to sit quite still and pretty throughout the Sabbath.

The **great angel** who rose in the East and commanded the winds to rest thus signified—according to those old astrological fables and paintings—the **seventh god**, or the presiding spirit <note>original: "Genius"</note> of the planet that was properly supposed to ascend the throne in the final age of the present world. However, our author designated him as the **Lord Keeper of the Seal** <note>original: "Obersten Reichssiegel-Bewahrer"</note> of the living God because he regarded the **Ram** <note>The constellation Aries</note>, or the **Lamb**, as representing Jesus, who (as previously stated) had reliably promised to restore the Jewish hierarchy <note>referring to the priestly government of Israel</note> and to enter into his reign shortly.

One should consider here that those astrologers who declared the constellations of the **Zodiac** to be the supreme gods, and who began counting them starting with the **Bull** <note>The constellation Taurus; ancient calendars often began the year when the sun was in Taurus.</note>, allowed the last of these—namely the **Ram**, or the **Lamb**—to ascend the throne at the end of the current world. Meanwhile, those who made the **planets** alone the supreme gods assigned the government of the final world age either to **Saturn** or to the **Moon**. It is clear to see that our author melted both opinions into one, and through a misunderstanding, interpreted them as the reign of his Master, whom he expected to arrive at any hour.

At the opening of the preceding seal—that is, at the beginning of the final <term>World Age</term> <note>original: "Weltalter"; a concept in historical theology where time is divided into distinct epochs or "ages."</note>—our author, as we have seen, had the dawn of the Great Sabbath announced by various heavenly signs, and had it immediately celebrated by the elect before the throne of the Lamb. Now, however, the final seal was opened. Consequently, the Great Sabbath, or the final age of the world, had to end now; that is, the final Great Day of Judgment had to break in with full force.

Since the author was indisputably a born Jew, certain Jewish ceremonies certainly had to be observed at its onset; for otherwise God might perhaps have become incensed and, in His grim zeal—as the prophets along with Moses depict Him—acted as if He were being trodden underfoot, so that even the author himself might have lost his little place in the New Jerusalem. Therefore, the High Priest—who appeared here, however, in the form of an angel—had to burn incense on the golden altar as a sweet aroma before the Lord at the opening of the final seal, and then have the conclusion of the Sabbath announced to the city, as was customary, by several Levites in the form of angels with trumpets. However, the fact that exactly seven such angels sounded their trumpets arose because the ancient <term>astrologers</term> <note>original: "Sterndeuter"; literally "interpreters of stars."</note>, from whom our author had learned his art of prophecy, attributed the seven chief deities,

to the planets, seven smaller subservient spirits were assigned, who then, to honor their masters—but each individually—sounded a bit of their trumpet, and in exactly the order in which they were arranged in ancient Egypt in former times according to their distance from the earth.

Just as some calendar-makers still today, for the sake of maintaining superstition, assign the rule over certain plants, animals, lands, rivers, etc., to each planet: so too did the ancient astrologers dedicate a certain class of activities to each. It is well known that in antiquity, these all consisted of three different principles: an airy one, a watery one, and an earthy one—or of spirit, soul, and body. The spiritual or airy principle came from the father of natural products, the Sun; the watery or <term>selenitic</term> <note>Moon-related; derived from Selene, the Greek goddess of the Moon.</note> principle from the mother, the Moon; and finally, the earthy or terrestrial principle from nutrients. Thus, the first two had a heavenly origin—that is, they were spiritual emanations of the two great lights of the world or their <term>genii</term> <note>original: "Geniuße"; guardian spirits or divine entities associated with celestial bodies.</note>—and therefore could not be destroyed, but had to endure eternally. But the third part <note>original: "Dritthel"</note> was certainly subject to decay or destruction: and for this reason, of course, only a third part of things could ever perish through the trumpet blast.

<header>### Revelation VIII.</header>
Finally, it should also be remembered that an ancient astrological fable caused the second world to perish by fire, after it had already long ago caused the first to be destroyed by water—that is, by a great flood.

When the first angel sounded the trumpet, the earthy third part of the trees and herbs was burned with blood-fire-hail because this trumpet blast was meant for the bloodthirsty Saturn, to whom both hail and the plant kingdom were consecrated.

But the second angel was the servant of bright-shining Jupiter, who took both the mountains and the sea under his special protection. Consequently, at the trumpet blast, a fiery mountain had to plunge immediately into the sea and burn up not only the earthy third part of all living creatures found therein but also the earthy third part of all ships; for in those days, these things also had a spiritual, a watery, and an earthy principle, and all things earthy simply had to be burned with fire.

Therefore, at the sound of the third trumpet, which rang out for the fiery Mars, a great star appeared in the sky, burning like a torch, and fell not only upon the earthy third part of the rivers but also upon the earthy third part of the sweet springs, all of which became bitter as a result.

Whenever the ancient <term>astrologers</term> and <term>priests</term> <note>original Latin: "Sacerdoten."</note> painted a symbol of the Earth, they also added the seven <term>planets</term> to it, specifically in such a way that four of them usually stood on one side and three on the other. In this way, people became accustomed to almost always dividing the planets into two small heaps, namely the heap on the right and the heap on the left. ...evil demons were necessary, who constantly rebelled against the good gods and ruined everything that the latter had made good. What? God would have found all his creatures "very good," and then out of revenge cursed the snakes? Would creatures be capable of offending the Creator, of making him angry, of feuding with him? Should one not loudly call this depiction of the Godhead blasphemy?

Accordingly, the fifth <term>trumpet-angel</term> <note>German: Posaunenengel; one of the seven angels who sound trumpets to signal apocalyptic events</note> was nothing more than the servant of Venus or the <term>morning star</term>. That is, according to the delusion of the <term>astrologers</term>, it was thrown into the well of the abyss, into the innermost regions of the earth, into the great furnace. In this way, there arose in the minds of the <term>Chaldeans</term> <note>An ancient people of Mesopotamia renowned in antiquity for their advanced knowledge of astronomy and astrology.</note>, who knew no greater river than the Euphrates, the "great stream" where the aforementioned four gods were said to be bound.

## Second Cont. of the third Vision

In a way, the author has once again violated the natural order and allowed those **seven thunders** to roar a little too early. They actually should have roared only now, when the servant of this **lowest planet** <note>In the ancient Ptolemaic system, the Moon was the planet closest to the Earth, and thus "lowest" in the celestial hierarchy.</note> blew the trumpet. For the same reason, the angel who was **clothed with clouds** and had a **rainbow** around his head should only have appeared to the author now, since these two attributes of lightning—the **meteors** <note>In the 18th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note> over which the Moon was said to rule—clearly pointed to that fact. Instead, he now suddenly has a song of triumph struck up in heaven, from the conclusion of which one can clearly perceive that the **twenty-four elders** were not blessed spirits, but merely the **twice-twelve constellations** of the northern and southern heavens. In high antiquity, these were regarded by the **Chaldeans** <note>The Chaldeans were an ancient people of Mesopotamia famous for their early developments in astronomy and astrology.</note> as the twenty-four judges of the dead and the living—that is, as the oldest overseers of the **black and white hours** of the day and night. Later, however, they were deprived of their dominion by the **astronomers**. According to the delusion of the weak, who took them for actual gods, they naturally found themselves quite offended by this, and now, at the end of the world, they rejoiced that the punitive judgments of the supreme God were breaking upon the **godless astronomers** who had changed the laws and, as it were, corrupted the world. Up to this point, our author has told the tales of the astrologers regarding the seven world ages, the destruction of the world, and the restoration of all things <note>Original: "Wiederbringung aller Dinge." Strictly speaking, he should have progressed immediately from the temple of God, which he saw open in heaven, to the new Jerusalem, the new heaven, and the new earth: for the other visions that he has related up to that point are all nothing more than fragments, which partly fit here and there into the remaining gaps of the already erected structure, and partly appear for a second time, only in a different form, and thus could easily have been left out altogether. However, he had once collected them with great effort without knowing that there were duplicates among them, and he was far too conscientious to withhold them from his readers.

Probably most of the images and tales that he has described so far originally came from Egypt, whereas those he describes in the following seem for the most part to have been invented by the Chaldeans and Persians, and for the most part contain the same meaning as those others indicated. But the Jewish-Christian <term>Gnostics</term> <note>A group of early religious seekers who believed that salvation was achieved through secret knowledge ("gnosis") rather than faith alone.</note> and <term>Manichaeans</term> <note>Adherents of a dualistic religion that viewed the universe as a struggle between the spiritual world of light and the material world of darkness.</note> certainly threw everything together and cooked up strange mixtures from it—at least our author did, who took the

What is to be made of the "voices from heaven," which were then in fashion among the Jews, is well known. Although it cannot well be denied that a divine power dwells within man, which at times speaks very loudly and presents to him partly distant objects and partly future events that directly concern him—in short, that many a person sometimes has premonitions—the superstitious Jews were nevertheless accustomed to exaggerate the matter far too much. They took every speaking idea that suddenly awakened in their over-strained imagination to be "voices from heaven." Among Christians, these are not infrequently held to be the effects of the Holy Spirit, especially among those whose awakened conscience torments them because of evil deeds. The Greeks called them the warning voices of the daemons <note>original: "Dämonen." In the classical Greek sense, a *daimon* was a guiding spirit or divine power, not necessarily an evil "demon" in the modern sense.</note>.

Our author seems to have learned the practice of eating books from Ezekiel, who likewise ate a parchment skin in his belly that was inscribed with "Lamentation, mourning, and woe" <note>A reference to Ezekiel 2:10 and 3:1-3.</note>; it tasted sweet as honey to him, yet it caused him no stomach cramps, presumably because it was not very large and fol-

The sweet taste indicated the pleasure one felt upon reading it, while the resulting stomach cramps signified the difficulties one had to overcome to "digest" the teachings contained therein, or to "tap out" the deeply hidden meaning of the <term>hieroglyphs</term> <note>The author uses "hieroglyphs" here to mean mysterious symbols or allegories rather than Egyptian script.</note> with which these books were usually inscribed. It is known, namely, that the ancient mysteries <term>mysteries: secret religious rites of the ancient world to which only initiates were admitted</term> were mainly of three kinds. Since the most ancient astronomers <note>original: "Sternseher"; literally "star-seers"</note> necessarily had to divide the sky from East to West into twelve roughly equal parts, owing to the twelve lunar revolutions that constituted the lunar year: thus the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Brahmins—from whom **Pythagoras** undoubtedly learned to recognize his hieroglyphs <note>symbolic or mystical signs used in secret societies</note> in the mysteries—taught that the entire heavens, which they certainly considered to be a regular hollow vault, were composed of twelve equal regular surfaces and were, consequently, a <term>dodecahedron</term> <note>a geometric solid with twelve flat faces, each a pentagon</note>. Its total surface, as is well known, consists of twelve regular pentagons. Now, this dodecahedron of the heavens was considered the dwelling place of the eternal light or the Godhead. Consequently, the regular pentagon was a sacred figure, and because of this holiness, not only did **Solomon** have the door to the Holy of Holies <note>the inner sanctuary of the Tabernacle and later the Temple in Jerusalem</note> made in a regular pentagonal shape, but **Pythagoras** also adopted this figure as a sacred hieroglyph into his mysteries.

### Third Continuation of the third Vision.

From all these teachings and hieroglyphs of **Pythagoras**, it now emerges beyond any doubt that natural religion <note>the belief in a creator based on reason and the study of nature rather than revelation</note> was his secret. For man, viewed as a spirit, is according to this teaching evidently an emanation of the eternal, uncreated spiritual light—or the Godhead—and must therefore not only endure eternally but also attain to higher perfections. This occurs if he properly utilizes the organs of the body given to him for the knowledge of the physical world in this life, strives constantly to be pure of heart, satiates his spirit with the sciences—especially with the knowledge of nature—and leads a divine way of life. These are certainly sublime, noble, and useful teachings, which for the most part were most urgently recommended by the founder of the Christian religion <note>Jesus Christ</note>, but were afterwards, alas, rendered almost insignificant by the bishops through all sorts of added opinions.

The **Pythagoreans**, then, were no more astrologers, fortune-tellers, necromancers, or alchemists <note>original: "Goldmacher," literally gold-makers</note> than were the initiates of **Ceres** <note>the Eleusinian Mysteries</note>. Deism or natural religion was their secret, and those symbols of the effects of nature, which they explained to one another, were merely its veils. But the planet-worshippers and fire-worshippers in **Egypt**, **Babylon**, **Persia**, and **East India** certainly did not have enough philosophy in their heads to realize that the hieroglyphs, symbols, and fables

<meta>catchword: the</meta>

---

<page-num>149</page-num>
### Revelation X. 8 — 13.

which their oldest ancestors had left them indicated nothing more than the workings of nature. They saw that from the course of the stars and from hieroglyphs, the falling and rising of the **Nile**, the times for sowing and harvest, solar and lunar eclipses, the conjunctions of the planets, and so forth, could be predicted with certainty. On this basis, they believed that future political changes of states must also be discoverable through these astrological images and periods. Often their prophecies actually came true by chance, and through this, they were strengthened in this delusion. Furthermore, they were the sole possessors of mathematics and physics, and could therefore perform thousands of illusions <note>original: "Taschenspiele," literally pocket-plays or sleight of hand</note>—all of which were regarded as sorcery—not only for the kings (who at that time knew nothing at all) but also for the simple people. Thus it happened that they were also regarded as so-called wise men or **Magi**.

Moreover, they worked alone in the field of chemistry and manufactured all sorts of remedies from herbs, which performed magnificent service in many illnesses and saved many people from death. Therefore, the profane <note>the uninitiated or common people</note> believed they possessed the secret of the gods and freed people at will from all diseases, as well as from death. Accordingly, the planet-worshippers and fire-worshippers indeed passed themselves off as great prophets, conjurers, physicians, and chemists <term>Scheidekünstler: literally "separation-artists," an early term for chemists or assayers who refined metals through chemical separation</term>. Thus, they had two types of deities, and yet only one type of secret, which granted them great prestige and much wealth. But it was precisely this profitability of their secrets, and these very differences in religious matters, that simultaneously caused great discord among them; out of resentment and envy over the advantages that one sect perhaps enjoyed over another, they mutually slandered and persecuted one another in the most horrific manner, as we shall clearly see in the following. For now, it is only necessary to note that the fire-worshippers considered the heavens—especially the Zodiac—to be the dwelling of the great God, the pure celestial fire; they made the constellations into subordinate gods, and on the contrary—to the annoyance of the planet-worshippers—declared the planets to be profane, alien gods who had unlawfully dared to intrude into the sacred dwelling of the fire, the Zodiac, to wander about and trample it.

One now sees clearly that the holy city in the Apocalypse <note>the Book of Revelation</note> is nothing more than the heavens. But why the heathens trample around in it for exactly forty-two months—that is, why the planets run around the Zodiac for exactly that length of time—I shall investigate further below.

Thus, our author viewed the ancient symbol of the heavens as an image of his holy city, and held the Zodiac to be the Jewish temple, while the middle strip of the Zodiac represented the inner court of the temple. However, he turned the four beasts of the solstices and equinoxes <note>the four cardinal points of the solar year</note> into four seraphim, a point on which the Gnostics <note>an early Christian mystical sect</note> agreed with him.

He had, moreover, read or heard something of the mathematical divisions of the Zodiac and the measurements of the stars, but unfortunately understood nothing of it. They were at the same time the first observers of the stars, and lived in regions that were bordered by mountains in the East and West; here it is to be noted that at that time far more mountains were volcanoes than now, which however for the most part gradually became extinct. Therefore these ancients saw the sun, their God, not only rise majestically every morning from behind a mountain, which perhaps simultaneously spat fire, but also sink down again every evening behind a mountain. For this reason, it happened that worship between two mountains became the fashion. But their children and grandchildren, who spread out into other regions where they found no such mountains in either the East or the West, and yet nevertheless retained the religion of their fathers, erected two columns or two obelisks at their camps and cities. These stood opposite one another from East to West and represented those two mountains behind which they had seen and worshipped the sun, their God, rising and setting in their fatherland. Gradually these two columns became the essential components of all temples of the sun; and where two such obelisks or pyramids stood, there was always a temple.

# Fourth Cont. of the third Vision

...walking among the Pillars of Hercules. Others also called them the Pillars of Hermes. And it is precisely these two mountains or pillars that the ancients used in such different ways, as I will soon show in more detail.

Undoubtedly, the earliest Europeans knew the earth from East to West no further than perhaps from Sina <note>In the 18th century, "Sina" (from the Latin Sinae) was a common term for China; the author uses it here to represent the easternmost edge of the known world.</note> to the Strait of Gibraltar, and thus let the sun rise daily from the ocean behind Sina, while letting it sink again behind the high rocks of the aforementioned strait: for they did not yet know that the earth is nearly spherical and rotates on its axis, but rather held it to be a flat lump, and truly believed that all the celestial bodies daily sank into the sea and rose out of it again into the heights. Since the sun, in their opinion, sank into the ocean at the western end of Europe, they imagined that Hercules had lived there. Therefore, they not only built him a temple there, but also made a high rock there into one Pillar of Hercules, while the other was unfailingly to be sought at the eastern end of the then-known world. But in later times, both were erroneously placed toward the setting sun, at the Strait of Gibraltar.

There is no reason to doubt that Hercules was in fact a symbol of the sun—

His fifty sons, whom he fathered with those fifty Danaids <note>In Greek myth, the Danaids were the fifty daughters of Danaus; the author interprets them here as a numerical allegory for the weeks of a lunar or solar year.</note> in a single day, were the fifty-two weeks of the year, which were changed into the round number of fifty and were certainly, as it were, fathered by the sun—except that the poets greatly exaggerated the matter, transforming a year into a day, and even into a night. His twelve heavy labors, which he had to perform at the command of Eurystheus <note>King of Tiryns, for whom Hercules performed his twelve labors.</note>, signified the course of the sun through the twelve signs of the Zodiac. The evil demons of the night, who were cast out from heaven, were compared to Philistines, among whom Delilah stood in high regard because she—or the moon—was also a goddess of the night. He toppled these pillars and collapsed the meeting house of the Philistines to kill himself and them: for at the end of the world, according to ancient astrological legend, the entire structure of the universe will collapse and kill all Philistines—that is, all the godless.

Since, moreover, the oldest peoples in the Orient were accustomed, as mentioned, to erecting a pair of such pillars or mounds at all their camps, hordes, and cities, Moses also used them as signposts for his nomads in the desert. Finally, the most beautiful olive trees grew on many mountains in the Orient. For this reason, the author compared the two mountains themselves to olive trees. Solomon had the capitals of the aforementioned two pillars decorated with pomegranates, which could perhaps also be taken for olives. Therefore, it is quite possible that the author could have taken the pomegranates for olives, and the two pillars—with their capitals and rings—for olive trees, or even for prophets.

### Fourth Continuation of the Third Vision, Revelation XI. 1–11.

...passes along the horizon, or, according to the opinion of the weak, sleeps in the ocean. Only during the day does it <note>Referring to the sun.</note> travel from East to West between its two overseers, the mountains, which consequently also only testify to it during the day; in the night, however, they lie as if dead in the streets, that is, on the horizon, where they are seen by only a few peoples living near them, but naturally are not laid in graves—for who would want to lay mountains in graves?

Here it should further be considered that a year in general does not always indicate a *solar year*, but often a *day*, a *week*, a *month*, a *century*, and so on: for this name generally means nothing more than a *period of revolution*, whether it lasts a long or short time. If, therefore, these years—as cannot be denied—were *Chaldean* <note>The Chaldeans were inhabitants of Babylonia, renowned in antiquity for their advanced systems of astronomy and astrology.</note> years, each of which consisted of twelve thirty-day months and several intercalary days <term>intercalary days: extra days added to a calendar period to keep it synchronized with the solar year</term>, though these latter days were not especially regarded by the soothsayers: then three such years and a half made exactly *forty-two months*, and exactly *one thousand two hundred and sixty days*, or exactly *one time, two times, and almost a half a time* <note>This is a reference to the cryptic chronological phrase "a time, and times, and half a time" found in the books of Daniel and Revelation.</note>; indeed, as I shall soon show, they even contained exactly the notorious *six hundred sixty-six*, and were thus the *keys* to all the important prophetic numbers that occur in the *Apocalypse* <note>original: *Apokalypse*; the Book of Revelation.</note>.

<column-break/>

In such a sleight-of-hand manner, the ancient *magi* <note>original: *Magier*; a class of Zoroastrian priests and scholars who specialized in astrology and the interpretation of signs.</note> and *soothsayers* hid their astrological prophetic numbers, and thereby gave the profane—who knew nothing of these silly secrets—reason to search for all sorts of *miracles* within them.

Since *forty-two months*, in the sense cited, make exactly *three and a half world-ages*, and thus signify exactly *half of the total duration of the world*: it becomes clear why those *magi* who considered *planetary worship* to be a sin allowed the *zodiac* <note>original: *Thierkreis*</note>, or the *celestial city*, to be trampled by the false gods—that is, by the *planets*—for exactly *forty-two months*. Namely, they saw them in the sky only at night and believed they would be driven away every morning by the fire <note>Referring to the sun's light.</note>. But the tradition of the *sevenfold duration of the world* was already in vogue among them, and for this reason, they counted only the *nights*—that is, exactly half of the total duration of the world, or three world-years and a half—for this duration of the stay of the profane in the celestial city.

Can one really make clothes out of the sun and put them on? In all our dear God's wide world, there is surely no tailor who can do that. But the moon is such a <term>master-of-all-arts</term> <note>Original: *Tausendkünstler*, a term for someone who can perform a thousand tricks or skilled feats.</note>. It certainly weaves its own garment from the light of the sun. However, one does not even need to fetch the allegory from so far away, as shall be made clear in more detail immediately.

When the ancient <term>Astrologers</term> in Egypt wanted to represent the fertilization of the moon, or of *Isis*, who then gave birth to vegetative nature, the *Horus*: they drew a young woman, and above her the sun, which surrounded and overshadowed her with its fertilizing rays. So that she might also be recognized by a certain attribute and not be confused with another goddess: she was placed upon a crescent moon, which was, as it were, her *pedestal*. Finally, to indicate that this woman was the queen of heaven, or the ruler of the twelve stars of the <term>Zodiac</term> <note>The belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs, which the author links to the woman's crown of twelve stars.</note>, a crown of twelve stars was placed on her head.

Thus, that apocalyptic woman, who appeared in a garment of sunbeams, and had the moon at her feet, on her...

### Fourth Vision

...on her head, however, she had a crown of twelve stars, was nothing more than the **full moon**, or the **highly pregnant Isis**, whom the ancient Egyptians believed was fertilized annually by the sun—by **Osiris**—and then gave birth to the young **Horus**, who represented rejuvenated nature. This young son, Horus, was afterwards made into the third person of the deity by these same ancient Egyptians, as we already know; and for this reason, it was said that immediately after his birth he was snatched away to God and His throne in heaven.

In primordial times, **China** <note>Original: *Sina*</note> was undoubtedly still connected to **Mexico** by a chain of mountains and high lands, allowing humans to spread out from Asia toward the rising of the sun as far as America. This is why the priests in Mexico have a fifty-two-year period, which clearly arose from the fifty-two weeks of the year and was brought there from Asia. They depict it in the form of a great serpent forming a ring or a wheel with four spokes. These four spokes signify the four seasons, while the serpent—which is also called the **dragon**—recoiling into itself is the well-known symbol of the constant duration of the solar and lunar revolutions. In the same way, the Egyptians represented the uninterrupted movement of the heavens from east to west under the image of a variegated

<meta>catchword: dragon</meta>

---

<page-num>171</page-num>
### Revelation XII. 1 — 17.

dragon that crawled back into itself in a circle. According to the interpretation of **Horapollo** <note>An author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs, likely from the 5th century.</note>, the colorful scales of this dragon signify the stars of the **Zodiac**. **Clement of Alexandria** also reports that the astronomers of these ancient nations represented the tilt of the solar and lunar paths under the image of several serpent coils. But be that as it may, this much is certain: in ancient times, the **ascending node** of the lunar orbit was universally called the **Dragon’s Head**, while the **descending node** was called the **Dragon’s Tail**, and in our calendars today these two moving points in the heavens are still called by those names. However, astrologers call that part of the lunar orbit where the moon has its greatest latitude—or where it stands furthest from the sun's path—the **Dragon’s Belly**. Now, in ancient times, just as today, all solar and lunar eclipses occurred at the nodes—that is, at the Dragon’s Head or Dragon’s Tail—and for this reason, it was said that the dragon sometimes ate the lights of heaven.

This charming allegory pleased the common people, who afterwards actually believed that a great, evil dragon was always sneaking around the sky and the air, and sometimes ate the stars, and even the sun and moon. Nations that lived in colder regions, where there were no dragons or flying lizards, but certainly wolves and bears,
