### Origin of the Superstition regarding Auspicious Sowing and Planting during the Full Moon.

So the dragon now stepped before the heavily pregnant Isis <note>In this interpretation, the Egyptian goddess Isis represents the Moon.</note>—that is, the shadow of the Earth fell upon the full moon, which was just about to pour out blessings with its light over the plants, or to give birth to vegetative nature, which was called Horus. The painful labor pains, which the woman is said to have had and made known with a great cry, were merely added by the ancients to make the allegory more complete. He, the dragon, wanted to devour the child once it was born: for he was considered an evil god, who sought to destroy the blessing of the good gods, and thus endeavored to ruin and devour the crops.

That the heathens, however, were made to be tended by this Horus—this young little son—with an iron rod <note>A reference to Revelation 12:5; the author suggests "tending with an iron rod" means living in a state of scarcity or harshness.</note>, came from the fact that the priests who invented this tale thought themselves better than the "profane," whom the author <note>Referring to the author of the Book of Revelation.</note> simply calls "heathens" out of Jewish pride. The Egyptian priests, whose entire theology was often nothing more than astrology, imagined that Horus was solely their god, who protected only their crops, while neglecting those of foreigners; in those foreign lands, he turned the earth into iron, so that neither grain
<meta>catchword: nor</meta>

nor wine would be produced in sufficient quantity, and consequently the people there were not infrequently "tended with an iron rod"—that is, he gave them little to eat and drink. Also, the dragon could not devour Horus: for he was the third person of the deity, and was caught up to the throne of the Highest, from which he returned annually to the earth, and thus, of course, never died completely, but only slept at times—about which one may read further in le Pluche <note>Noël-Antoine Pluche (1688–1761), a French priest whose work "History of the Heavens" explained mythology through physical and agricultural realities.</note>.

After the eclipse was complete, the moon descended below the horizon, and for this reason it was said that Isis had descended from heaven in distant regions and fled to a desolate place, where she would be nourished for exactly half the duration of the world, or three and a half world-ages—that is, forty-two world-moons, which make exactly one thousand two hundred and sixty great days: for the moon, taken as a whole, is actually below our horizon just as often and just as long as it is above it, and must therefore spend three and a half out of seven whole world-ages in the desert, while passing through the sky above us for the remaining three and a half.

When our old wives look at a solar eclipse in the water as if in a mirror, so as not to blind their eyes, and perhaps disturb its surface with their movement, they often say: "Oh, how the dear sun defends herself! How she trembles! How she fights!" Now, the ancient astrologers, who did not yet know the use of smoked glasses <note>Glass darkened with soot to allow for safe viewing of the sun.</note>, likewise observed this phenomenon on trembling water surfaces, as if in mirrors, and believed that the sun was trembling. For this reason, the fable of the sun’s struggle during eclipses gradually arose.

The kingdom of the whole heaven, on the other hand, would be given to the chosen, the holy people, and all power would serve and obey the Most High!

They divided this duration into four different smaller world ages, because the four principal constellations of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>Literally "circle of animals"; the belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs</note>—the Lion, the Scorpion, the Water-Bearer, and the Bull, in which the points of the solstices and equinoxes formerly lay—seemed to require it, and because in this way, the four world ages could be conveniently compared with the four seasons.

Three constellations of the zodiac were assigned to each season: and for this reason, the symbols of the four world ages were given a tripartite <note>German: "etwas Gedrittes"; likely referring to the grouping of three signs into a single astrological 'quadrant' or season</note> quality.

# Revelation XIII 1 -- 8. 11. -- 18.

...regarding these, which likewise amount to half of the entire duration of the world, the following is to be noted.

Chaldeans <note>An ancient people of Mesopotamia, often associated with advanced early astronomy and astrology.</note> and East Indians made use of three periods for their astronomical works and their astrological spider-webs—as **Syncellus** <note>George Syncellus, a 9th-century Byzantine chronicler.</note> knows from **Berosus** <note>A Hellenistic-era Babylonian writer and priest of Bel.</note> of **Abydos**—one of which was called **Saros**, the other **Neros**, and the third **Sossos**. The **Neros** contained six hundred solar years. The **Sossos**, however, contained only sixty of them. Finally, the **Saros** consisted of the **Neros** taken six times, and thus amounted to exactly three thousand six hundred solar years, which therefore make up exactly half of the seven-thousand-year age of the world, if one, as is customary, uses the round half-thousand instead of those six hundreds. Now, some transcribers of the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> are said to have written only six hundred and six instead of six hundred sixty and six. If, therefore, the latter reading is correct, one clearly sees that the astrologers merely added the second factor, six, to the **Neros** (or six hundred), but wisely did not indicate that one should multiply the two together. Yet, in order to perhaps entirely palm off their astrological junk in a clever way, or to hide the nocturnal duration of the beast a little more, they may well have added the **Sossos** to the **Neros**, and merely added that sec-

<column-break/>

# Fifth Vision.

-ond factor of the Saros at the end without a multiplication sign; in that case, those corrected six hundred sixty and six indeed emerge, which now evidently contain three thousand six hundred solar years, or the nocturnal duration of the seven reigns of the planets.

Herein, then, lay the great wisdom which was required for the consideration of this number of the beast: magnificent wisdom! I, however, know of none other than that which shows the means and teaches how to use them rightly, whereby the welfare of mankind and the perfection of the whole is powerfully promoted—not with mysterious, unintelligible chatter that darkens people's heads, but in an understandable way.

These consist of large, medium, and small stars: consequently, the large ones must have sung the **bass**, the medium ones the **tenor**, and the small ones the **discant** <note>The "discant" refers to the highest vocal part in early music, equivalent to the soprano or treble</note>, because otherwise one could not see how their voices could have resembled not only the bass-like thunder, but also the tenor-like roaring of water, as well as the lovely discant-like sound of harps. But that the stars were truly said to have sung in former times was taught long before our author by **Pythagoras**, who knew how to demonstrate the music of the spheres so naively with great acclaim; and I fear in no way that much can be blamed in my explanation of the new song of these chosen ones.

From the **conjunctions** of the **planets**, the ancient **priests** <note>original: *Sacerdoten*; Latin for priests</note> made amorous **rendezvous** <note>original: *Rendez-Vous*; French for a meeting or tryst</note> of the gods and goddesses, because they either no longer understood the true meaning of the images handed down to them by their great-great-grandfathers, the oldest stargazers, concerning such celestial events, or they intentionally used them to hoodwink the people. Such **rendezvous**, however, the constellations cannot give to one another: for these never leave the houses that have once been assigned to them, and consequently never come to the women, as perhaps the **planets** do. ...henceforth they are indeed still bachelors, or virgins, and have never defiled themselves with women or with men. — Could this astronomical misunderstanding have perhaps even given rise to the so highly praised practice of **celibacy**, since not only the Apostles but also the **Gnostics** <note>The Gnostics were early Christian-era dualists who often valued spiritual purity over physical existence</note> so greatly preferred the invisible heaven with its chaste multitudes over the wanton pagan gods, and undeniably held a very great influence on the doctrines of the early Church?

The **four beasts** <note>original: *vier Thiere*; often translated as the "four living creatures" in Revelation</note> are here again the four principal constellations of the **Zodiac**, which the author already saw in heaven at the beginning of his second vision, and now allows to appear once more; just as the **twenty-four elders**, who reappear here, signify those twice-twelve stars of the northern and southern skies, or the ancient rulers of the days and nights.

As for the **three angels** who fly one after another through the midst of heaven to announce—partly the arrival of the great **World Judgment** <term>Last Judgment</term>, or the beginning of the new kingdom of the highest God; partly the fall of the wanton **Babylon**; and partly the punishments of the worshippers of the Babylonian seven-headed beast—they were unfailingly first devised around the lifetime of our author by the Gnostics and by the predecessors of the Persian Magus, **Mani** <note>The text refers to "des Mannes" (the man), likely a wordplay or reference to Mani, the founder of Manichaeism</note>, and were interpreted by our author out of

### Sixth Vision

The City, which here signifies the entire Heavens, is again divided into those three well-known parts into which it has long been partitioned: one containing the stars of the **Zodiac** <note>original: "Thierkreis"</note>, another containing the stars on this side of the Zodiac, and the third containing the stars beyond the Zodiac.

However, the kings of the earth will likely not allow themselves to be stirred up to war against God by these frogs in any way.

### Seventh Vision

Now the kings of the earth gather with their armies by the Beast to fight against the leader of the heavenly hosts, who is just now riding the beautiful white horse <note>original: "Schimmel" — referring to the white horse mentioned in Revelation 19:11.</note>. But the Beast is seized, and with him the false prophet as well. Now they are both thrown alive into the pool of sulfur. The others, their helpers, are slain by the sword that comes from the mouth of the Word of **GOD**, and all the birds are sated on their flesh.

Has the angel perhaps correctly explained the Beast and its rider to the author? Let us see!

He says first that the Beast *was*, and *is not*, but would come again out of the abyss and go into hell. Immediately after, however, he says it *was*, and *is not*, even though it *is*. This is certainly not spoken in an angelic manner <note>original: "englisch" — a pun in German, as the word means both "English" and "angelic." The author is mocking the illogical nature of the angel’s statement.</note>: for according to any *ontology* <term>ontology: the branch of philosophy dealing with the nature of being and existence</term>, Being and Non-being are two contradictions that God himself cannot reconcile, because Being necessarily always cancels out the possibility of simultaneous Non-being. But perhaps this angel was from a fairyland where a special god ruled, for whom reconciling contradictions was mere child's play.

<column-break/>

<page-num>237</page-num>

### Revelation XVII — XVIII — XIX

Still, I must help this angel along—who was undoubtedly not yet correctly oriented regarding the true astronomical sense of the old monstrous images—and pull him out of the embarrassment in which he has thoughtlessly entangled himself with his contradictions. To be sure, at that time the Beast had already *been*, and *was not*: for it signified nothing more than the *tapestry* <note>original: "Tapis" — likely referring to a ritual cloth or symbolic diagram used in secret societies or ancient rites.</note> of the lesser *mysteries* of the Babylonian magicians, who were by then already scattered, could no longer celebrate their *mysteries*, and had lost their secret images. It had therefore *been*, and *was not*. But since it actually represented the world with all seven planets, especially their duration, in a mysterious way, it still truly existed in the *original*, and was thus merely lost in the *copy*, as the world certainly still stood at that time.

In the seventh age of the world is the Great Sabbath, or the thousand-year reign of the *Messiah*, whom the Jews created from the *Horus* <note>A reference to the Egyptian deity Horus, suggesting the author believes biblical figures were derived from older Egyptian mythology.</note> of the *Egyptians*. Consequently, the Beast must not show itself there, but must meanwhile remain stuck in the abyss. But when the planets have completed their great *revolutions* <term>revolutions: here referring to the completion of great astronomical cycles or orbits</term>: then all the world, and consequently this Beast too, must appear before the judgment, where it must then certainly be condemned to the eternal pool of sulfurous fire, because at that point the world—or the *original* of this Beast—is known to be destined to burn.

Thereupon the angel said that the seven heads of the beast were seven mountains on which the great harlot had firmly seated herself. But these seven mountains were further intended to mean seven kings, of whom five had already been, while the sixth currently possessed the empire, and the seventh, by contrast, was yet to come, only that he should not rule for long at all. In this explanation, there is no contradiction. Rather, it fits quite well with the doctrines of the Gnostics <note>Gnostics: early Christian sectarians who sought "gnosis" (secret knowledge) and often blended Persian, Jewish, and Greek philosophies.</note>, who forged together the misunderstood astrological images of the Babylonians, Egyptians, Persians, Jews, and Greeks and applied them to Christianity. But one must understand the seven kings as the seven planets upon which the later Magi of Babylon founded their mysteries, as if upon seven mountains. "Five of these kings have already fallen" means nothing more than that five entire world-ages or millennia, over which the first five planets ruled, have already passed. Under the rule of the sixth, people were still living at that time, although they already expected its end at any moment, as the dawning of the Great Sabbath—the beginning of the thousand-year reign of the Messiah—seemed to the Jewish-Christian-Gnostic visionaries <note>original: "Gesichtersehern" — a slightly mocking term for those who see visions or "faces" in their trances.</note> to be standing daily at the door. The seventh king could therefore not actually ascend the throne at all, because the Messiah contested it with him. Nevertheless, he was once included in the prophetic image of the world's duration,

contained, and they did not dare to cast him out entirely: for by doing so, the image would have lost its prophetic value, and he, the king himself, might perhaps have taken it badly, indeed even started a bloody war with the aforementioned Messiah. From this, it is clear why he, when he comes, may only stay for a short time.

But that the beast should be the eighth king, and yet simultaneously belong to the seven, is where the angel contradicts himself again, and shows very clearly that he did not understand the very first principles of thought: for every quantity is equal to itself; consequently, the eighth unit cannot be of the seven, but must belong to the eight. Yet one must not look for mathematical accuracy in his discourse at all, and not hold it against him that he violates it so greatly. The angel took the ten horns to be ten kings who were only just to receive the kingdom, burn the great Babylonian harlot, and finally themselves succumb to the Lamb in battle. In this matter, he is quite correct again, only that he takes each century of solar years—which in high antiquity was always counted as the lifespan of a king—as a king himself, and thus mistakenly substitutes ten kings for ten royal lifespans. The ten horns therefore mean, as stated, nothing more than the ten centuries of the duration of the reign of each planet. From this, it is easy to see that actually every head of the beast has ten horns—a fact, of course, that was not told to everyone <note>original: "nicht Jedermann auf die Zähne band" — a German idiom meaning one did not explain it plainly or make it common knowledge.</note>, because the secret could have been betrayed all too easily by it. These horns certainly had to receive the kingdom: for the last thousand-year world age, or the reign of the last of the seven planets, was only just about to begin.

With the passing of these last ten centuries, the entire present world was to come to an end in fire. Consequently, the Babylonian whore also had to descend into the lake of sulfurous fire with them. Also, at the end of the current great planetary re-

To be sure, these last ten centuries had already been given to the kingdom of the Messiah, who now, according to the angel's interpretation, also had to succumb along with the Lamb—which simply did not work, because in such a case he would have had to subject himself to himself. However, this did not matter to the issue, and people did not feel any pangs of conscience about overlooking such trifles, so long as they found a means to inject a truly mysterious meaning—one that well suited the hobby-horse <note>original: "Steckenpferde" — a favorite obsession or pet theory</note> of the Judeo-Christian taste of that time—into these astrological images.

# Seventh Vision

...the city itself, however, and particularly the merchant class, had not taken any special interest in it. One should not be surprised, however, that the Jews of this city especially wished for every conceivable evil, rejoiced quite heartily over its decay, and found its downfall so palpably evident in those fantastic astrological images. For at that time, they possessed vengeful spirits that had not yet been shaped by any good moralists, but were instead provoked to the most loathsome bitterness by the holy "Huron-songs" <note>The author uses "Huron-songs" as a derogatory comparison between ancient Hebrew prophecy and what 18th-century writers perceived as the "savage" or "primitive" war-chants of Indigenous North Americans.</note> of the prophets. Of the entire eighteenth chapter—which the author has cobbled together from the harshest passages of all the Jewish prophets and has an angel recite—I wish to mention nothing at all. <header>Revelation XX.</header>

My body will indeed be dissolved in death, and in the form of its vapors will enter the atmosphere, where it immediately falls back down with the rain, fertilizes plants, nourishes all kinds of cattle, and then attaches itself once more to human flesh; I shall probably have to argue quite a lot over this flesh on that great day of judgment if I should want to have it back again. However, the inventors of that supernatural <term>restoration of all things: the doctrine of *apocatastasis*, the belief that all creation will eventually be returned to its original, perfect state</term> certainly did not know this natural resurrection of the flesh, nor could they have known it, since they based their entire natural science merely on astrology, which allowed all things to come into being anew from the spiritual emanation of the stars in every new world according to the laws of constellation—thus, our doctrine of the resurrection of the bodies of the dead arose from those old fairy tales of the astrologers regarding the restoration.

As for what the author says elsewhere concerning the first and second death, and the first and second resurrection, it deserves no special investigation; it is already sufficiently clear from what has preceded why he calls eternal damnation the "second death," and why the resurrection of the prophets for the thousand-year kingdom must represent to him the "first resurrection," while the resurrection of all the dead for the final judgment represents the "second resurrection."

> Serpent! between this woman and you, between her descendants and your brood of serpents I will put enmity! The descendants of this woman shall crush your head, but you shall bite them in the heels.

Of his creation story I want to mention nothing at all: for it reveals too much that at that time the mathematical sciences were still completely asleep, and consequently let human understanding grope in the dark with all five senses.

The first human pair seems, in his work as in the *Zend-Avesta* <note>The primary collection of religious texts of Zoroastrianism.</note>, to be a figurative representation of the <term>heliacal rising</term> <note>The first time a star or planet becomes visible in the dawn sky just before sunrise after having been hidden by the sun's glare.</note> of the <term>Gemini</term> <note>The constellation of the Twins.</note>. The eastern one always rises somewhat earlier than the western one, as the latter seems to emerge, as it were, from the side of the former. "Sleeping," in the context of the stars, means lying hidden in the sun's rays or below the horizon. "Awaking from sleep" for them means appearing visibly out of the sun's rays or above the horizon. When, therefore, the oldest sky observers wanted to represent the successive rising of the twins, they painted a pair of humans who were just waking from sleep, and let one spring from the side of the other. The Tree of Wisdom was therefore the sun here, because it gives light—the Tree of Life, on the other hand, was the moon, because according to the delusion of the ancient astrologers, it breathes the means of life onto the earth.

In this, the oldest poets and Moses <note>The traditional author of the first five books of the Bible (the Pentateuch).</note> certainly all agree that the first humans were supposedly as happy as gods; but they differ from him in that they let this divine bliss last for a very long time. From this, it can be sufficiently inferred that the traditions of the "ages of the world" and of the "golden race of man" may all have arisen from those ancient pictorial reports of the <term>heliacal</term> <note>The first appearance of a star or planet in the dawn sky before sunrise.</note> rising and setting of the golden stars.

The very first humans must, of course, have existed at some point; but they were certainly, through many generations, so little different from the other animals that it would have been impossible for any reports of them to have reached their descendants, in whom reason and culture were beginning to awaken.

We now come to <term>Jacob's prophecy</term> <note>Referring to Genesis chapter 49, where the patriarch Jacob blesses his twelve sons on his deathbed.</note>, which is fundamentally nothing more than an Egyptian allegory of the twelve constellations of the <term>Zodiac</term>, regardless of the fact that an anonymous author in the third volume of the *History of the Royal Academy of*

Judah, the lion, signifies here the <term>Momphta</term> <note>In early modern Egyptology (such as the works of Athanasius Kircher), Momphta was considered the Egyptian name for the spirit or deity associated with the constellation Leo.</note> of the Egyptians, or the Lion of the Zodiac—one constellation is skipped here because the previous two brothers only make up one—In ancient times, the agricultural year in Egypt began with the entry of the sun into Leo, that is, with the <term>heliacal</term> <note>The first appearance of a star or constellation in the dawn sky just before sunrise.</note> rising of <term>Anubis</term> or the Dog <note>The star Sirius (the Dog Star), whose rising coincided with the annual flooding of the Nile.</note>, because at this time the Nile rose over its banks, flooded the land, and gave it fertilizer for the growth of grain for the new year. For this reason, the Lion was granted supreme dominion over the flooding of the Nile and over the remaining constellations of the Zodiac; therefore, indeed, all the children of his father—that is, all the animals of the heavens—now had to bow before him. He was at the same time, because of his overwhelming strength, the king of the animals: and for this cause, he broke the necks of all his enemies with his paws. In the heavens, even in high antiquity, he was drawn not as a standing lion, but as a quietly reclining one. Therefore, it is said quite correctly that he had knelt down and couched like a lioness, who had just returned from battle as a great victress and was eating her prey in peace. ->Zebulun! You shall dwell at the haven of the sea, and at the haven of ships!<- <note>Genesis 49:13.</note>

This means you shall dwell on the shores where the crabs and storks reside: for this allegory refers to the constellation of Cancer <note>The Crab.</note>, which the Egyptians composed of a stork and a crab.

The Virgin <note>The constellation Virgo.</note> had to be left out entirely, because the flooding of the Nile fell under her reign. She was therefore joined to the Lion, from which the <term>Sphinx</term>—that is, the lion with a maiden's face, or the ancient symbol of the duration of the flooded Nile—was created.

The bony donkey <note>Genesis 49:14 describes Issachar as a "strong ass" or "bony donkey."</note> carried burdens: the Scales or **Omphra** <note>Omphra likely refers to an Egyptian term for the measurement of land or the constellation Libra (the Scales).</note> also carried some. > Dan shall be a serpent by the way, an adder in the path! He shall bite the horse's heels, so that its rider shall fall backward! Lord, I wait for your salvation! <note>Genesis 49:17-18.</note>

In Egypt, **Typhon** <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian god Set, often associated with chaos, storms, and the desert.</note> was composed half of a serpent and half of a scorpion, so that the figure then closely resembled the shape of a dragon, which was not only a great enemy of all the stars, as we have seen above, but

also undertook to oppose both the generation and the growth of all earthly creatures. Thus, this whole allegory of the serpent that was to bite the horse in the heels referred to **Typhon**—that is, to the celestial Scorpio—under whose reign in the land where the twelve signs of the zodiac were first painted, dangerous diseases raged, and where the whole of vegetative nature, as it were, died every time. "Lord, I wait for your salvation" means nothing more than that the supreme God will eventually heal the damage that the Bull receives from the Scorpion.

> Gad, you are armed! You shall lead the army, and lead it around again! <note>A variation of Genesis 49:19: "Gad, a troop shall overcome him: but he shall overcome at the last."</note>

Among the Egyptians, the Archer <note>The constellation Sagittarius.</note> was dedicated to **Nephthys**, who was appointed as overseer of the armory of **Osiris** (or the Sun) and was depicted in the form of a centaur with a drawn bow in his hands. Consequently, he was always armed and had to lead the army of the Sun—that is, the stars of the zodiac—around and around again in the heavens.

->Asher! From you comes rich bread,<-
->And you shall show yourself pleasing to kings!<-
<note>A translation of Genesis 49:20. In the biblical text, Asher is promised fertile lands.</note>

**Pan** or **Mendus** <note>Referring to the Ram of Mendes, an Egyptian deity often associated with fertility and later equated with the Greek god Pan.</note> was the **Goat** <note>The zodiac sign Capricorn.</note> among the Egyptians and was responsible for the harvest; for most grain in Egypt ripened when the sun entered this constellation. Accordingly, the Goat or **Pan** certainly provided bread, and he showed himself pleasing toward kings—that is, toward the gods—because he allowed them to benefit from the harvest through the offering of the firstfruits.

->Naphtali! You are a swift<-
->hind, and you speak smooth words!<-
<note>Genesis 49:21. The German "Hirsch" (deer/stag) is used here, though the biblical Hebrew is usually translated as "hind" (a female deer).</note>

This allegory actually refers to the **Water-Bearer** <note>The zodiac sign Aquarius.</note> of the Egyptians, specifically to **Canopus**, who took the form of a water bucket upon which a human face could be seen. However, how **Jacob** or **Moses** could attribute the swiftness of a deer and pleasant, smooth speech to this water bucket, I cannot say. One would have to assume that swiftness here signifies the fleeting nature of the hours, which were measured with flowing water. Thus, the smooth speeches would indicate the gentle, uninterrupted, smooth flow of these water clocks. <note>The author is referring to a clepsydra, an ancient device that measures time by the regulated flow of liquid.</note>

All of this fits perfectly with the **Ichton** <note>Likely a derivation of the Greek "Ichthyes," meaning fish; referring here to the zodiac sign Pisces.</note> of the Egyptians, that is, the constellation of the Fish. **Ichton** was the image of all the innumerable things that the earth brings forth from her maternal womb. The infinite multitude of these things was traditionally indicated by fish, which likewise multiply in an inconceivable manner and lay almost infinitely many eggs. "You will grow as if by a spring" therefore means: you will increase greatly and show very fruitful daughters, who will bear more and more children. The Archers who rise up against him are nothing more than evil spirits who sometimes oppose growth or fertilization but nevertheless never overcome the **Ichton**. "Blessings from heaven" signifies the dew and the gentle Egyptian rain. "Blessings from the deep" represents the fertility of the fields or the soil. > ->**Benjamin**, you are a ravening<-
> ->**wolf**! In the morning you shall<-
> ->devour the prey, and at evening<-
> ->you shall divide the spoil!<-
<note>A translation of Genesis 49:27. In the author's astrological framework, Benjamin represents the final sign of the cycle or is linked to the transition of the stars.</note>

Since the **wolf** is the wicked animal that always displays a great appetite for sheep, the ancient **star-gazers** <note>German: *Sternseher*; refers to early astronomers or astrologers.</note>—who observed the heliacal setting <note>A heliacal setting occurs when a star or planet disappears into the brightness of the sun's rays at sunset.</note> of the heavenly **Ram** <note>The zodiac sign Aries.</note>—placed a **wolf** next to the sheep who devoured it. This was done to indicate that the **Ram** in the heavens would be invisible for a few months every year. Regarding this ravening **wolf**, it was later fabled that in the morning, shortly before sunrise, he devoured all the other stars from the sky like sheep; in the evening, however, he penned them all back into the sky again, undigested. **Moses** or **Jacob** therefore took him away from the **Ram** and compared him to **Benjamin**, who was said to devour the little sheep in the morning and give them up again in the evening. It is clear that this allegory certainly fits the heavenly **Ram**, whom the **Egyptians** idolized in the form of a man with ram’s horns under the names of **Ham** or **Ammon**. <note>Referring to the Egyptian deity Amun or Amun-Ra, often depicted with ram horns; "Ham" is a biblical reference to one of the sons of Noah, traditionally associated with Egypt.</note>

# regarding the Messiah.

Of this sort are nearly all the prophecies that appear in the Bible—the men of God did not know the true astrological meaning of their prophetic sayings themselves. They took the metaphorical reports of the ancient star-gazers for revelations from the gods, who had made the fates of men known to the initiates, or to the priests and prophets, under the dark veil of such images in the Mysteries. Furthermore, one sees from this anew that these images must have seemed just as old to the Egyptian scholars of that time as they do to us. God knows whether **Moses** did not forge the entire history of **Abraham**, **Isaac**, **Jacob**, and his twelve sons entirely from the Egyptian deities. At the very least, it evidently bears the stamp of the genealogy of the three deities of generation and those twelve gods of the **Zodiac**.

Regarding the **Passover Lamb**, it is to be noted that at the time of its institution, the **Ram** <note>Aries.</note> was precisely in its heliacal setting and was, so to speak, killed. It always sets heliacally in the evening; consequently, the **Passover Lamb** had to be slaughtered immediately after sunset and eaten during the night. > A star shall come out of **Jacob**, and a scepter shall rise out of **Israel**. This one shall crush all the princes of the **Moabites** and scatter all their children! **Jacob** shall become a ruler and destroy all cities! <note>Numbers 24:17.</note>

But before he becomes wise, the land before which you tremble must mourn for its two kings! Isaiah 7:14, 15, 16. <note>The author is quoting a variation of the prophecy regarding Immanuel, often interpreted by Christians as a prediction of Jesus’s birth.</note>

This is yet another allusion to the young **Horus**. As is well known, the celestial Virgin in Egypt was dedicated to **Isis**, the mother of **Horus**, and to the moon. She gave birth to him annually when the sun passed from the Virgin <note>The constellation Virgo.</note> into the Scales <note>The constellation Libra.</note>. However, as long as the sun remained in those two kings of heaven—the Lion <note>Leo</note> and the Virgin—**Isis** remained pregnant with **Horus**, and all the good land lay desolate under the overflowing Nile. That is to say, the land was, as it were, completely abandoned by the two stars or kings who ruled during the aforementioned flood. — But the prophet himself did not know that the young woman was **Isis** and **Immanuel** was the young **Horus**; therefore, he fashioned from the latter a Jewish Messiah, a Jewish benefactor, and turned the two celestial kings of the Egyptians into two kings of Judah and Israel.

### Prophecies

...[all fle]sh shall see that the Lord is God! Isaiah 40:3, 4, 5.

Here our visionary makes use of the secret teachings of the Persian Magi <note>Followers of Zoroastrianism, known for their focus on the struggle between light and darkness.</note> concerning the future reign of the Sun, or of the pure heavenly fire. He had heard that at the end of the present world, this fire would resume its dominion—which had been snatched from it by the godless planets among certain peoples—and would then abolish all disorder, level all mountains, and raise all valleys. Therefore, he resolved to compose a prophecy for his nation based upon this idea.

The Lord, for whom the way was to be prepared, was the Sun, for which the constellations pave the way from the East toward the West, as it were. The prophet in the wilderness was thus not John the Baptist, but a Magus in Persia; and that Lord, for whom the constellations were to prepare the way, could not signify Jesus, but rather had to signify the Sun.

He was wise and highly exalted because the most ancient Egyptians had made him the third person of their Trinity. ### concerning the Messiah.

-ing Horus can be seen in *le Pluche* <note>Noël-Antoine Pluche (1688–1761), a French priest whose work "Histoire du ciel" sought to explain the origins of mythology through astronomy and agriculture.</note>, where one will also find some of his enemies depicted. Consequently, his appearance was indeed at times exceedingly hideous, and it may well be that our soothsayer saw him in this form, but found no particular pleasure in it.

However, Horus did not suffer all these illnesses, or even death itself, as a punishment for his own debts—for he was holy, wise, and just—but merely for the benefit of humanity. According to the delusion of the ancients, humans had unfortunately become mortal through the <term>Fall of Man</term>, and thus required food that they could not produce for themselves. Therefore, he bore the burdens of men; that is, he died annually and, through his death, imparted to all hungry sinners the blessing which they afterwards harvested. Therefore, he "sprouts before the Lord"—that is, before the Sun—out of the soil and upward, like a fresh shrub from its root, as often as he rises again from the dead. Indeed, all Egyptians, like stray sheep, would have cried out in vain for food if they had not had the dear Horus, who every year, for the sake of their needs, allowed himself to be killed quite patiently like a lamb and buried beneath the mud of the Nile.

"He is cast into the earth like the poor, and dies like the rich" means nothing more than: the seeds are scattered into the earth like the poor dead—or like the <term>profane</term> <note>original: "Profanen," those not initiated into sacred mysteries.</note>, who are neither stars, nor prophets, nor initiates, and are buried without pomp. But they die away in order to then appear in a far more magnificent garment, and to bear many children, to carry much seed—that is, to bestow great wealth upon the heirs.

**Horus** truly never acquired this great wealth through deception or unjust usury, but rather took it from the soil and from the lovely dew of heaven. After he was killed and then resurrected, he bore fruits and seeds through which he lived eternally, and which beautified his lineage from year to year through countless branches.

Since he gives his life unto death—that is, since the seed falls into the earth and dies—he certainly receives many and strong children; that is, the land certainly brings forth much grain and good wine.

Nonetheless, this entire chapter is supposed to contain a prophecy regarding the suffering, the burial, and the resurrection of Jesus. However, how could Jesus have been buried as a poor man and died as a rich one? How? Did they bury him

# regarding the Messiah

"His going forth has been from the beginning and from eternity" <note>A reference to Micah 5:2, traditionally interpreted as a prophecy of the Messiah's eternal nature.</note> means: **Horus** has already been begotten and born every year since the beginning of the world, indeed from eternity. > Lord, I have heard your judgment, which terrifies me! Lord, you bring your work to life in the midst of the years, and make it known in the midst of the years! **Habakkuk 4:2.** <note>The biblical Book of Habakkuk contains only three chapters; the author is likely citing Habakkuk 3:2.</note>

The ancient Egyptians began their year at the heliacal rising of the Dog Star <note>Sirius; its "heliacal rising" occurs when it first becomes visible in the dawn sky just before sunrise.</note>, that is, with the entry of the sun into Leo. Whenever the sun passed through Capricorn and Aquarius, the crops became ripe; that is, whenever Horus became fully active and truly alive. Now, however, Aquarius is six constellations—that is, half a year—removed from Leo: consequently, in Egypt, God certainly brought his work to life "in the midst of the years" every time.

That in this passage the prophetic meaning is truly to be sought in the words "in the midst of the years," or in the middle of the times,

<column-break/>

<meta>catchword: See</meta>

Were this correct, one would not need to seek any prophetic meaning in the entire passage; for all living creatures come to life *during* the years, and never *outside* of the years.

> But you, daughter of Zion, rejoice greatly! You, daughter of Jerusalem, shout for joy! See, your king comes to you as a righteous one and as a helper, but poor, on a donkey and on the foal of a donkey! **Zechariah 9:9.**

It was upon these two donkeys that **Zechariah** now placed the Messiah, the king who was to free the Jewish land from the heathens, and had him enter Jerusalem upon them. Otherwise, Horus was not "poor," except when he slept: but precisely because he rode no mule, but merely a pair of donkeys, he must certainly have appeared poor to our soothsayer <note>The author uses "Wahrsager" (soothsayer) rather than "Prophet" to diminish the spiritual authority of the biblical text.</note>.

# Prophecies

> "Behold, there is a man whose name is Zemach! <note>Hebrew for 'Sprout' or 'Branch,' a messianic title.</note> Through him everything shall grow, and he shall also rebuild the temple of the Lord." **Zechariah 6:12.**

Here Horus or Zemach appears—that is, a young sprout as a prophet, or as a listener of the Lord who allows everything to grow, and consequently also rebuilds the temple which Nebuchadnezzar had ordered to be burned—However, this saying has also been presented as a prophecy regarding Jesus, even though it should rather have been interpreted as referring to Cyrus <note>Original: 'Kores'; the Persian king who ended the Babylonian Captivity.</note>, who actually had the burned temple rebuilt.

Is it then to be presumed that **Jesus** would have told this cousin and bosom friend—who undoubtedly often discussed with him the aforementioned new Kingdom of Heaven, brought so near by astrologers and soothsayers—nothing of his great undertaking?

"Ha!" some will object, "then these bosom friends would surely have quarreled over the Messiahship <term>Messiat: the status or office of being the Messiah</term>! Neither would have wanted to be the forerunner!"

But the Scripture said the Messiah must come from Judah. Now, John, as the son of a priest, belonged to the Levites <term>Leviten: the tribe of Israel traditionally responsible for priestly duties</term>: consequently, he could absolutely not become the Messiah. Jesus, on the other hand, as a son of Joseph, sometimes counted himself among the children of Judah, and it is clear that the two could not quarrel over the Messiahship.

So the matter was decided. The prophets had said: "See, in the wilderness is a prophet's voice, preparing the way for the Lord! And see, I send my cherub <note>A reference to Malachi 3:1, where the messenger is sometimes interpreted in light of angelic imagery</note> before me to pave the way!" Therefore John had to represent this angel. Jesus, on the other hand, followed him soon after in his teaching office and with his miraculous signs. Both undoubtedly had the noblest intentions, although error and exaggerated enthusiasm were linked with them. But what great and noble deeds are ever done with completely cold blood? How often does truth and good not come from error?

Who in Persia was accepted into the realm of the pure heavenly light of the highest God—that is, into the Mithraic mysteries <term>Mithrageheimnisse: a Roman and Persian mystery religion centered on the god Mithras, which involved secret initiation rites</term>—was first baptized. This was intended to show that the

# 328 Jesus and | his Disciples 329

...put on clothes, and then faithfully follow the Hierophant <term>Hierophant: a high priest or interpreter of sacred mysteries</term>—who ruled them all like a great king in the name of Mithras <note>Mithras was the central deity of a mystery religion practiced in the Roman Empire, which shared themes of rebirth and ritual washing with early Christianity</note>—with modest chastity in all things. The Jewish Gnostics combined this mysterious effect of the baptismal ceremony with their dark astrological fancies regarding the impending end of the rule of the planets and the future Kingdom of the **Messiah**. They introduced the baptismal ceremony of the Persians into the Jewish land even before **John**, though they could not achieve great prestige with it because they still treated it as a special secret in the Persian manner, and only baptized those who wished to join their specific sect.

**John the Baptist**, on the other hand, who believed that the Kingdom of the **Messiah** had come very near—indeed, that the **Messiah** himself already walked the earth—now invited all people to this kingdom with his baptism. He even accepted the brood of snakes and vipers, the Pharisees and Sadducees, as members of this new kingdom, albeit reluctantly. Thus, **John** was no fraud, but merely a pious fanatic who had so deeply immersed himself in the Mithraic mysteries and the astrological fancies of his holy prophets that even the most rational philosophy could not have awakened him from this systematic dream. This is much like many today who believe they have found all sorts of important secrets in the hieroglyphs of the an-

<meta>catchword: cients</meta>

---

# 329

-cients, and in the prophetic passages of the Bible, and who even build entire systems upon them. They cannot be convinced of the contrary of their opinions by any philosophy, nor even by mathematical demonstrations.

In the same way, **Jesus** was also no fraud, but a true friend of humanity. However, he had likewise become so entangled in the dark teachings of the Persian Magi <note>original: "Magier"</note> as well as in the dreams of the astrologers and the divinations of the prophets of his nation, that he found himself fully convinced of the certainty of his status as Messiah. Yet, at the same time, he wove into his system of teaching an excellent morality, which certainly had a very beneficial influence on the human race. Because of this, every rational man must still love him exceedingly and hold him in high esteem with heartfelt gratitude.

Since he held himself to be the **Messiah**, we must consider him from four different points of view: first as a **Moralist**, secondly as a **Miracle-worker**, thirdly as the **King of the Jews**, and fourthly as the **Son of God**. We shall therefore go through these four perspectives closely, one after the other, and dwell a little on each.

As a moralist, he deserves, as mentioned, the greatest respect and love of mankind, primarily because he lowered himself to the lowly with his teachings, presented them clearly to them, preached them with captivating enthusiasm, and even dared publicly before the **scribes** <term>scribes: scholars and experts in Jewish law, often depicted in the New Testament as rivals to Jesus</term> to assign a far higher value to virtuous actions than to sacrifices and the hypocritical disfiguring of faces. <note>original: "Verzehrungen der Angesichter"—likely an archaic usage or error for "Verzerrungen" (distortions/disfigurations), referring to Matthew 6:16 where hypocrites make their faces look miserable while fasting.</note> That he taught superhuman or even entirely new moral truths, however, cannot easily be maintained. > What you wish that people should do to you, that you must also do to them!

Among the Jews and pagans, who did not yet have proper hostels and inns <note>In the 18th century, the lack of a modern hospitality infrastructure in the ancient world was a common point of discussion among historians.</note> where everyone could have obtained food for money at any time, this precaution was very necessary; in the books of the Old Testament, one always finds that the bread bags were the first concern whenever people wished to travel. Is it then conceivable that these five and four thousand men—who had come to Jesus from as far as a day's journey, even with women and children—would have completely forgotten their bread bags and bread baskets? Who would not have regarded a morsel of bread from Jesus—from this great prophet whom the people truly had to love and admire for his beautiful speeches—as the most magnificent of delicacies? Because of the mystical concepts that the ancients held regarding the Pythagorean five, the planetary seven, and the zodiacal twelve <note>The author suggests that the numbers of loaves (5 and 7) and baskets (7 and 12) in the Gospels were chosen for their symbolic or numerological significance in ancient philosophy and astrology, rather than being literal counts.</note>, one might almost cast suspicion on the five and seven loaves, as well as the seven and twelve baskets. However, in doing so, one might do our historians too much of a grievance and unlawfully accuse them of superstition.

Perhaps it will be objected that the five thousand men would not have wanted to make Jesus their king if he had performed no miracle before their eyes? Yet, did he not share, as it were, his last morsel of bread with them? What poor and lowly people would not gladly want to make a king of someone who shares his last bite with them and, in his speeches, condescends to them as affectionately as Jesus did, if they were allowed to?

Perhaps it will further be objected that the Evangelists themselves were eyewitnesses to these miraculous deeds and could not possibly have told an untruth. But how then can Matthew speak of two possessed men <note>original: "zween Rasenden" – literally "two raving ones," referring to the demoniacs in Matthew 8:28.</note> who are said to have come out of the burial caves of the Gergesenes into the herd of swine, while Mark and Luke know of only one, who was called Legion? One is, after all, essentially different from two? Matthew must therefore have said something false, either care-

lessly or intentionally and with purpose. If one does not wish to admit this, then Mark and Luke must either be mistaken or knowingly lying. This or that remains true as long as someone can prove to me that one and two are equal to each other. Now, if two Evangelists could either have erred regarding the number of the so-called possessed or intentionally told an untruth, then three of them could also, in regard to the miraculous feeding of the five and four thousand men, either have intentionally deceived the world or, out of superstitious weakness, been deceived by the people themselves before their very eyes. — Luke, in any case, has everything merely from hearsay, as he himself expressly reports <note>A reference to the prologue of the Gospel of Luke (1:1-4), where the author admits to compiling accounts handed down by others.</note>, and saw nothing of it himself.

At the wedding at Cana, that good wine, which was said to have been water, probably consisted mainly of the juice of sweet fruits, which Jesus poured into the jars before he had water added to them. Let us assume the latter case. Did Jesus therefore have to be the true God? I cannot yet believe it!

Certain reliable experiences have convinced me that we do not yet by any means sufficiently know the powers of man, and also that man, by virtue of these high powers, is indeed capable of producing incomprehensible effects that can be demonstrated before one's eyes <note>original: "ad oculos"</note> neither from our compendiums of physics nor from all our philosophical tomes; it is only that these powers never become alive in the vast majority of people, especially phlegmatic ones, but merely show themselves active at times in a few fiery seekers of truth and friends of humanity. But one must not misunderstand me. I am not saying that such incomprehensible effects are supernatural: for everything that happens there happens from natural causes, from natural forces. But do we then know the manner in which natural forces act? Do we know how the soul acts upon the body, the body upon the soul, light upon our visual organ, our visual organ upon our inner senses, or gravity upon bodies?

Experience must count for more here than reasoning <note>original: "Raſonnement" — abstract logical deduction or theorizing.</note>. Furthermore, I am not saying that some humans, by virtue of their powers—which for the most part are still very hidden from us—are capable of making impossible things possible, such as perhaps even raising the dead; or that they could heal severed limbs that have long since scarred over, or turn winter into summer, wood into iron, water into wine, a donkey into a rationally speaking animal <note>A reference to the biblical story of Balaam’s ass in Numbers 22.</note>, and so forth! In these matters, at least, my experience has certainly always taught me the opposite. But this it has also taught me: that some people can heal various fevers and cramps, not only through simple touch—which is linked to a truly intense, benevolent urge of the soul—but can even effect some small changes in the atmosphere itself through truly vivid wishes during bad weather; indeed, even without their will and without their assistance, they can often clearly perceive events occurring among their sympathizing loved ones and friends. Most remarkable of all is surely the story of **Lazarus**, whom Jesus is said to have raised from the dead. We must therefore examine it somewhat more closely than the other **miracles**.

**Matthew**, **Mark**, and **Luke** say nothing at all about it, which undoubtedly must arouse some suspicion against the account, since it is said to have happened in their presence and is certainly the strongest proof of the divinity of Jesus, if it has a firm foundation. On the other hand, **John**—who alone tells the story and undoubtedly possesses the most learning among all the **Evangelists**—seems not to have paid much attention to miracles: for he relates only a few of them and instead treats his readers at greater length with the person and the mysterious teachings of his Master, using that **mystical tone** which was then in fashion among some **philosophical sects**. One has reason, therefore, to give more credence to the few miracles described by this man, as a **philosophical mind**, than to those innumerable wonders found described in the three other unphilosophical **Evangelists**. In ancient times, such a precaution was undoubtedly unthinkable for this nation, as anyone could easily walk out of the grave if they came to their senses again. In this way, one or another may have occasionally returned from death to life back then, and in this way, the prophets may have raised many a deceased person from the dead. Was the **youth of Nain** perhaps not really dead either? Was he perhaps merely in a state of stupor? <note>The original German "Hinbrüten" suggests a lethargic, comatose, or trance-like state rather than biological death.</note> Did chance lead **Jesus** to **Nain** precisely at the time when this unconscious, seemingly dead youth was being carried out? Three **Evangelists** are completely silent about this highly important event. **Luke** alone tells it. For this reason, it certainly seems very suspicious: for **Luke** is very fond of piling miracle upon miracle and is, by all appearances, all the more superstitious because he himself witnessed none of them, but, as he himself reports, merely received the accounts from those who were there from the beginning and saw all the events. <note>A reference to the prologue of the Gospel of Luke (1:1-4), where the author admits to using secondhand accounts.</note>

Those of the first class are either invented by the **Evangelists** or carried out through the cunning of women. <note>The author uses the term "Weiberlist" (women's cunning), a recurring theme in his argument that female followers of Jesus staged miracles to support his ministry.</note> To this belongs, for example, the raising of **Lazarus**; the story of the **youth of Nain**; **Peter** walking on the deep water; the healing of the man with dropsy on the **Sabbath** to the offense of the **Pharisees**; **Peter’s** great catch of fish.

Those of the second class belong to quite common occurrences which, however, have been much too far exaggerated by the unphilosophical <note>In this context, "unphilosophical" implies a lack of scientific or critical reasoning.</note> **Evangelists** and only made into miracles by them. # Jesus and

<page-num>370</page-num>
<header>Jesus and</header>

Those of the third class, finally, are indeed true miracles, since they cannot be explained by our common principles of physics, and generally cannot be demonstrated by any universally recognized principles; but for that very reason, they nonetheless belong to the effects of nature and by no means arise from supernatural forces, but merely from natural ones. It is only that we are capable of perceiving them more through the senses of the soul than through the sensory organs of the body. To this class belong the alleviation of paralytic fits; <note>The original German "Gichter" refers to gout, but in this historical context, it was often used for various forms of paralysis, fits, or "the palsy."</note> the calming of convulsions, or the casting out of demons; the stopping of the twelve-year issue of blood, as well as the raising of the young girl, and that calming of the stormy sea waves—provided these last two miracles do not perhaps belong to the second class.

It is also to be noted here that it is not known whether Jesus’s authoritative commands always achieved the desired effect with all the sick, or whether those who recovered fell into relapses, <term>Rezidive<gloss>A medical term for a recurrence of a disease or a relapse after an initial recovery.</gloss></term> and some even returned home without any help at all. The latter is very much to be suspected, since even John 7:3–5 shows that his own physical brothers would believe neither in him nor in his miraculous deeds. But let us now proceed to the third point of view, from which he appears as the **King of the Jews**.

In former times, **Horus** <term>Horus: An Egyptian deity often associated with the sun and rebirth in ancient mythologies.</term> laid himself in the grave in Egypt when the sun approached the celestial **Lion** <note>The zodiac sign of Leo.</note>. In Mark, on the other hand, it simply says: then Jesus sighed in his spirit and said: "Why does this generation want to see a sign? Truly, none shall be given to it!" and in Luke he says again: "This is a wicked kind: it demands a sign from me. But

Therefore, that explanation—*just as Jonah lived for three days in the belly of the shark, etc.*—was likely only added as a literary embellishment <note>original: "hinzugedichtet". The author suggests that the author of the Gospel of Matthew added this specific detail to align the story with later Christian dogma.</note> by Matthew, and was not actually added by Jesus himself. Luther translates it: *just as Jonah, etc., so too will the Son of Man remain for three days and nights in the heart of the earth.* But even if we assume Jesus had actually added this explanation to his words, and indeed in this latter sense, it would not correspond to the actual outcome for two reasons. Firstly, he did not remain in the grave for three full days and nights, but only for one day and about one and a half nights. Secondly, if he had known that he would truly die and rise again after three days, how could the Scribes and Pharisees have taken his resurrection as a sign, since he supposedly revealed himself after his resurrection not to them, but only to his disciples? How could the Scribes consider something a miraculous sign of which they knew nothing?

If Jesus did not mean the Temple here, but rather heaven: then he would not have needed to say: "You cannot come there now!" If one wants to follow someone to heaven, in the usual sense, one must lose one’s life anyway, and there is no need to make a solemn vow of it first. How could Jesus have replied to that: "Would you really want to lay down your life for me?" No one can ask such a thing who does not wish to be defended by someone with life and limb. But how can he, who is losing his life voluntarily, desire assistance against death—or at least not say that no sword should be drawn on his account?

Horus the Egyptian <note>The author is likely drawing on 18th-century "Mythicist" or "Rationalist" theories that sought to find the origins of Christian figures in Egyptian mythology, specifically the cult of Isis and Osiris.</note> was the Messiah of the Jews, as we have often shown. Specifically, he represented the bread of life and wine of life; that is, he was food for the soul and drink for the soul, heavenly food and heavenly drink. Jesus knew all of this. He further knew that he would now, in any event, enter into a different relationship with his disciples, whether he succeeded in his intentions for the Temple or not. For this reason, he now gave them bread and wine figuratively, instead of his body and blood, to eat and drink in memory of the fellowship he had maintained with them until then—and thus the Lord's Supper was instituted.

We proceed finally to the fourth point of view, which presents Jesus to us as the Son of God.

That he gave himself out to be the Son of God does not need to be proven, for the Orthodox <note>The "Orthodox" refers to traditional, conservative theologians who uphold the literal divinity of Christ, as opposed to the "Rationalist" authors of this era.</note> teach this themselves, and one could cite more than a hundred scriptural passages that clearly demonstrate it.

**As** a wonder-worker, Jesus likewise reveals himself in the form of a great man who, by means of his strong power of imagination, works incomprehensibly upon nature in small ways, but especially upon the dispositions of men—and thus, through their dispositions, also upon their nerves and their bodily fluids <note>Original: *Säfte*. This refers to the "humors," an old medical theory suggesting that the balance of fluids like blood and bile determined health and temperament.</note>. One simply cannot and should not deny all so-called miraculous works that he is said to have performed, if one does not wish to cast aside the historical credibility of all historians. However, it is certain that the Evangelists greatly exaggerated most facts, and often mistook quite ordinary occurrences for miraculous works, and not infrequently deceived themselves: for this becomes clear from a comparison of their own reports. Things that Jesus may have occasionally brought about through the secret power of his fiery imagination, and by virtue of the lively or vivid faith of those in need of help, thereby setting all the people in astonishment, were nonetheless natural effects of entirely natural, though not generally known, forces. Jesus considered these forces supernatural and believed that God was working through him in a very special way. His disciples believed this too; and so did most other people. This common delusion <note>Original: *Wahn*. In this context, it refers to a shared misconception or a powerful illusion rather than insanity.</note> of the masses certainly promoted the spread of better Christian morality immensely. ### 432 Jesus and | his Disciples. 433

...or if we may entirely trust the Evangelists in this matter: then he was, as has been shown above, at least uncertain within himself whether the three-year state of his public **humility** <note>original: Niedrigkeit; referring to Jesus's earthly ministry before his exaltation.</note> was meant to signify that three-day death, or whether he would have to dwell alone for three days in the Temple of God in order to arrange it in a new way, or whether he would finally, in fact, dwell bodily in the grave for three days before he would be permitted to establish the **Kingdom of Heaven**—that is, the eternal **Universal Monarchy** <note>A common Enlightenment-era term for a world-spanning empire, here applied to the Church's political ambitions.</note> that was to extend over heaven and earth. — This did not, to be sure, happen through him himself; but his **vicars in Rome** <note>original: Statthalter zu Rom; referring to the Popes as the representatives of Christ.</note>, those first-born **children of light**, understood the matter well. They applied every effort to truly establish this universal monarchy—taken in both a spiritual and worldly sense—long after the passing of their Lord. — They also established it successfully, but in doing so, they merely forgot to take its eternal duration into account. — After the **children of this world** <note>A biblical contrast (Luke 16:8) between the secular-minded and the spiritually-minded.</note> had long been forbidden from using the **weapons of light**, and consequently had often been forced to "crawl to the cross" <note>An idiom meaning to submit or apologize under pressure.</note>, they finally became wiser than the children of light. They had **twelve- to twenty-four-pound arguments** <note>A clever metaphor for heavy artillery/cannons, which were categorized by the weight of the cannonballs they fired.</note> cast, against which the masters of the spiritual and worldly universal monarchy certainly have nothing more to object.

<column-break/>

As the **Son of God**, Jesus does not distinguish himself favorably either. To be sure, he says himself: "Fear God above all! Honor your parents! Love your fellow man as yourself: then you shall be saved." But he treats his mother most **contemptuously**, never calling her "Mother," but rather "**Woman**." Even more! The Evangelists even seem to credit it to him as a merit that he was "subject" to his parents as a boy. Was that a merit? Was that not a duty? He disowned not only his father but also his mother; we have seen this clearly above. He recognized no father other than God, and no mother or siblings other than those who followed him. He did not even recognize David as his great-ancestor, but rather considered himself to be **David’s Lord**. All of this was brought about by his **astrological system** <note>The author argues Jesus’s self-conception was based on an esoteric or astrological interpretation of Messianic prophecy.</note>. The Christian Church thus trusts merely in **Matthew** and **Luke** <note>original: Matthäussen und Lukassen; archaic German plural forms.</note> and directly contradicts its own author when it teaches that Jesus was begotten of God and born of Mary: for he had nothing to do with that woman who passed him off as her son, because in his own opinion, he was born **directly from God**.

### 434 Jesus and | his Disciples. 435

...let the Evangelists themselves answer. We must, in any case, shed a little light on the character of the Evangelists and other known disciples; and so the answer to the above question will emerge of its own accord on this occasion.

**Matthew** and **Luke** base their concepts of the Messiah, and their reports of **Jesus**, entirely on those Jewish prophets who [foretold] the Messiah; <note>The German text here seems to have a small omission in the original printing, but the context implies a contrast with Mark.</note> [Mark], by contrast, narrates simply what he has either seen and heard, or believes he has seen and heard, quite simply, and without consulting the prophets about it, much less interjecting his own philosophical reasoning. Only about once does he cite a prophetic passage that, in his opinion, was fulfilled in **Jesus**, and regarding the origin of his master, he reports nothing at all, except that **Nazareth** was his birthplace or his hometown. **John** agrees with **Mark** in that he also does not recognize **Bethlehem** as his master's birthplace and does not personally appeal to the prophets: but in exchange, he seems to treat the history of his master all the more according to his **Gnostic philosophy** <note>A diverse group of early religious movements that emphasized secret knowledge (gnosis) and often viewed the material world as inferior to the spiritual; the author suggests John's Gospel is more mystical than historical.</note>, and thus distinguishes himself quite considerably not only from **Mark**, but also from the other two Evangelists.

That Matthew and Luke not only invented his various genealogies <note>original: "Ahnenverzeichnisse"</note> but also the strange occurrences that are said to have happened—with Gabriel at his conception, with those shepherds at his birth, after his birth with those Magi from the East <note>original: "Magiern aus Morgenlande"</note>, and with Herod—entirely out of their own heads.

The story of the **outpouring of the Holy Spirit** <note>The event of Pentecost described in Acts 2.</note> is considered by our **author of the Fragments** <note>Hermann Samuel Reimarus, who argued that the Apostles fabricated many events to maintain their status.</note> to be entirely fictional. # Europe's Modern Enlightenment. #

The completely crude state of the uneducated nomad, who knows no advantage other than physical strength, and the flourishing of agriculture, livestock breeding, manufacturing, trade, the arts, and the sciences, are indisputably the two opposite boundaries of the culture of the human race. The flourishing of agriculture, livestock breeding, manufacturing, trade, and the arts mainly strengthens and beautifies the body, as these things grant sensory pleasure. The flourishing of the sciences, however, primarily elevates and sharpens the soul. Therefore, the culture of man can aptly be divided into two different stages: a lower and a higher one. On the lower stage stand all new inventions that noticeably promote sensory pleasure, or even just comfort; on the higher stage, however, stand only the sciences that promote the growth of the spirit <note>The author uses "spirit" (Geist) here in the Enlightenment sense, referring to the intellect and rational mind.</note>. In the future, for variety, we will often call the lower stage simply *culture* <note>original: "Kultur"</note>, and the higher stage, by contrast, *enlightenment* <note>original: "Aufklärung". This distinction between material "culture" and intellectual "enlightenment" was a major topic of debate among 18th-century German philosophers like Moses Mendelssohn and Immanuel Kant.</note>. Culture can exist among many peoples without enlightenment needing to show them its beautiful face. But where the latter is to show itself publicly, the former must necessarily have already prepared the necessary dwellings for it, and all—

...have made good arrangements, because Enlightenment is the daughter of Culture, and therefore receives its life, as well as all its needs, from its mother.

Now the first question is: Has the world, or at least Europe, gained in culture and enlightenment since the introduction of Christianity?

Scholars who diligently study the Greeks and Romans, but in doing so neglect not only the modern sciences and arts themselves, but also their history, claim almost universally that the Greeks and Romans were already just as clever, just as learned, just as wise, and just as enlightened long before the emergence of Christianity as we are. Indeed, it is even claimed that we are nothing more than parrots <note>original: "Papagaien"</note> who babble everything after the ancients, but never think for ourselves; and that we must indeed babble after them if we wish to produce anything good, because they have already exhausted the source of the good and the beautiful. This is often proven with that saying of the famous Solomon, who already in his lifetime claimed that nothing new happens under the sun <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 1:9, a common trope used by traditionalists to argue against the possibility of true progress.</note>. In such a way, we would not even be as clever and as enlightened as the Greeks and Romans who lived before Jesus, if their affected admirers were right, and if we really merely imitated, but did not reflect for our–

<meta>catchword: after=</meta>

---

<page-num>469</page-num>

-> # Enlightenment. # <-

<sig>Ii 2</sig>

selves. Nevertheless, these same admirers of antiquity also often claim that Christianity has contributed a great deal to the culture of the human race in Europe. But how could it have promoted this culture if we were not more cultured, and more enlightened, than the ancient Greeks and Romans?

However, these scholars, these partisan admirers of antiquity, act against themselves—or at least against their fellow colleagues who are well-versed in the modern sciences—with obvious and supreme injustice. They do so because they do not understand the matter any better, and because they neglect the modern sciences. Even assuming our philosophers could not reach, much less surpass, a Pythagoras, a Socrates, a Plato, a Zeno, an Epicurus, and so on; assuming our poets were no Homers, no Anacreons, no Virgils, no Horaces, and so forth; assuming we had not only no Demosthenes and no Cicero, but no orators at all: would it then follow that we therefore have less culture, less enlightenment, than the ancient Greeks and Romans? I cannot yet believe it. Such a conclusion would certainly be too hasty. We must properly examine all branches of the arts and sciences before we are permitted to draw a conclusion.

<header>470 Europe’s Modern</header>

<meta>catchword: Didactic-</meta>

Most of the high-sounding poems of the ancients merely fill the imagination <note>original: "Phantasie"</note> with beautiful images and pompous words, which instill no truths and no clear—often no correct—concepts into the understanding. Instead, they merely tickle the ear or enliven the power of the imagination, and thus stand merely at a lower stage of culture, especially since they grant only sensual pleasure while not concerning themselves with truth. From this, however, it is clear that all nations, no matter how little enlightened they might be, could have good poets, provided that nature in their homelands always offered them enough objects and a wealth of necessities. They would certainly not lack for suitable words and names for these things very soon, since languages in all places that are rich in all kinds of things form quite easily by themselves.

The art of poetry <term>Dichtkunst: The 18th-century term for the craft of writing poetry and literature.</term> will therefore not do much harm to Enlightenment, but it will also not particularly promote it, because no poem is considered beautiful if it presents naked truths clearly. If one did not already know that poets for the most part do not tell the truth, but rather seek only to present the objects of their songs to the senses as pretty, charming, and beautiful, then their works would necessarily harm higher culture. Indeed, they very often do harm it in unphilosophical minds, which is proven by the perverse effects of most of our modern novels, but even more by the fanatical consequences of ancient astrological poems.

<meta>catchword: Therefore</meta>

Didactic poems and satires can certainly help to enlighten the understanding; however, what these do well is ruined again on the other hand by many other genres of poetry. For this reason, the art of poetry, as stated, can only grant high pleasure to unphilosophical readers. From this it must further necessarily follow that modern Europeans would nonetheless not be inferior to the Greeks and Romans in Enlightenment, even if they did not come anywhere close to them in the art of poetry. This, however, I do not even wish to assert, because poets might take it ill, and because, according to my limited insight, many of them really do not yield much to Horace, nor Virgil, or others.

Demosthenes and Cicero <note>Famous orators of Ancient Greece and Rome, respectively.</note> did not convince the people with their magnificent speeches; they only persuaded them. But anyone who can be persuaded must surely not necessarily be cultured, much less enlightened, and does not examine everything precisely? An enlightened head never lets himself be persuaded; rather, he weighs everything exactly and then seeks out the truth or probability for himself. But the less Enlightenment and the less culture prevails among a people, the more easily they allow themselves to be persuaded—experience certainly teaches this very clearly.

Thus, the great effects that *Demosthenes* and *Cicero* were able to produce with their speeches may well do little honor to the Greeks and Romans in regard to their *culture* <term>Kultur: Here meaning the level of social refinement or civilization.</term>. Enlightenment requires nothing but clear truths that walk about quite naked, without rhetorical splendor, and force themselves upon the understanding whether it wishes them to or not—Eloquence, on the other hand, must put beautiful clothes on the truths it recommends; that is, it must dazzle the eyes with a glittering shine for the people whom truth is supposed to please. This procedure presupposes, however, that among such *nations*, the *culture* of the understanding has certainly not yet made great *progress*, because people there do not want to see the truths themselves, but merely the golden tinsel, the magnificent stones, and the colorful clothes with which the orators deck them out, and wish to receive them with the clapping of hands.

Sensual pleasure, therefore, still has the upper hand among such people, and consequently displaces the spiritual pleasure that springs from the enlightenment of the understanding; and from this it is clear that the true happiness of mankind has likewise lost nothing from the fact that the great orators of antiquity have for the most part been lost. Indeed, perhaps something has even been gained, if one excludes pulpit orators <note>original: "Kanzelredner"</note> who know how to present virtue to the people in dazzling garments. Now people in the East and West, in the South and North, can conveniently and cheaply communicate their painstakingly acquired knowledge and arts to one another in many thousands of copies! Now, a cruel persecutor of the sciences may once again commit several public libraries to the pyre: yet a thousand copies of every good book still remain in the world! A reference to the Pope or the high Catholic hierarchy, whose authority the Enlightenment authors often challenged.</note> can any longer forbid the use of reason with emphasis and effect! The first great blessing that flowed to the world from the art of printing and the enlightenment resulting from it was the Reformation of Christianity. Although one cannot exactly attribute to the Reformation itself any great *immediate* merit regarding the freer use of reason, it nevertheless showed Europe's <term>Potentates</term> <note>Sovereign rulers or monarchs.</note> how they could withdraw themselves from the supremacy of the Roman See <note>The Papacy in Rome.</note> and how they should apply those riches—which had to be paid to the Holy Father for the forgiveness of sins or other such things—to a better use in their own countries.
