Germany, therefore, has actually kindled these first lights of modern culture and Enlightenment for all of Europe—yet without its own merit, but purely by chance and because of its physical nature—even though it felt the bright pulses of this light later than Italy and France. Certainly, these countries had to move ahead of the German Empire in culture and industry by great strides: for they were more conveniently located for trade, and possessed a more enticing climate for the encouragement of the spirit than our fatherland, which grants the spirit of its nation only slow growth, but all the more strength, like its oaks. <note>The author uses the common 18th-century metaphor of the German character being slow to develop but sturdy and enduring, much like the German oak tree.</note>

### Thoughts on the Vocation of Man through God.

That there is a God, nature teaches us very emphatically in things small and great. We must therefore briefly consider nature before we can form a correct, albeit weak, concept of the greatness and goodness and glory of its Creator. Let us begin with the creation.

If we were to put our globe together a million times and make a new sphere from it, this sphere would almost equal our sun in size. **Saturn** is a thousand times, and **Jupiter** over one and a half thousand times larger than our globe. **Saturn** has five, and **Jupiter** four moons <note>At the time of this writing, astronomers had identified the four Galilean moons of Jupiter and five of Saturn's moons (Titan, Iapetus, Rhea, Tethys, and Dione).</note>, each of which is many times larger than the moon which orbits our globe. **Mars** is also nearly as large as the <term>wandering star</term> <note>original: "Wandelstern"; an archaic term for a planet.</note> we inhabit, as is **Venus**; only **Mercury** is seventeen times smaller. But if one were to melt together all these celestial bodies—which are all similar to our Earth and most likely also inhabited by humans—along with their moons, and cast them into a single sphere: it would still be only about six

Therefore, all the planets of our solar system, taken together with their moons <note>original: "Trabanten"</note>, are to be regarded as almost nothing against the sun: for out of six hundred, one can lose one without feeling any noticeable loss in the total sum. If one could stack thirty Earth-globes on top of each other, one would reach as far as the moon’s orbit; but in the sun, one would have to stack a hundred Earth-globes on top of each other to get from one edge of it to the other. Consequently, the Earth-globe could quite comfortably stand inside the sun, and its moon could swing around it without hitting the edge, even if the moon were three times further away from the Earth than it actually is. We rightly consider our wandering star <note>A poetic term for a planet.</note> to be very large: for its circumference amounts to five thousand four hundred <term>geographical miles</term> <note>A German geographical mile was roughly 7.4 kilometers or 4.6 modern miles, based on 1/15th of a degree of the equator.</note>; but compared to the sun, it is to be regarded as almost nothing. But if it were as large as the sun, its circumference would amount to five hundred and forty thousand large miles. Thus, if a person could travel ten miles a day on the sun, he would still need one hundred and twenty years to circumnavigate it.

Such suns now exist in the world in an infinite multitude: for all stars—excepting some that are called planets, and some others that only show themselves occasionally and are called comets—are such suns; indeed, many of them even surpass our sun many millions of times over. The entire **Milky Way** consists of nothing but such suns, which appear so close together, and represent, as it were, only a pale white haze <note>original: "Duft"</note>, merely because they are indescribably far away from us and, in view of our standpoint, stand more behind one another than next to one another: for in reality they are all unspeakably far away from each other. We must take pains to imagine their great distances from each other somewhat more clearly.

The <term>astronomical yardstick</term> <note>original: "Elle," literally an ell or cubit, used here as a standard unit of measure.</note> is quite large and is called the **radius of the Earth** <note>original: "Halbmesser der Erde"</note>. It contains eight hundred and sixty large miles and is used only when astronomers measure the worlds and their distances from one another. Now, our sun is approximately twenty-two thousand such Earth-radii away from us. **Saturn** stands ten times further away from it and thus swings around the sun at a distance of approximately two hundred and twenty thousand radii of the Earth, or nearly two hundred million geographical miles. This is indisputably a great distance in our eyes—

People whose sight carries sharply into the distance can look across six, and sometimes even seven, such **celestial steps**, each of which, as stated, is nearly eighteen thousand million Earth radii high. Specifically, it is customary to divide all suns or <term>fixed stars</term> <note>Stars that appear not to move relative to each other, as opposed to "wandering" planets.</note> into six different classes according to their apparent size: the stars of the first size are counted in the first class, stars of the second size in the second, stars of the third size in the third, and so on. Now, the stars of the second size stand just as high above the stars of the first size as the stars of the first size stand above us or our sun. Whether at one time there were no suns or worlds at all, or whether they have instead existed from eternity in their matter and only suffered certain changes from time to time, is not difficult to decide. I assert the latter, and indeed not only from the nature of the worlds themselves, but also from the concepts that we must form of the divine attributes—We wish to ascend from the small to the great.

One says: everything is transient. All experience teaches us this. Men, or rather human bodies, are conceived, born, and pass away. Trees grow and rot. Even gemstones and metals are subject to transience. Thus, our entire globe consists of things that are subject to transience and never last forever; consequently, they not only could once not have existed, but they will one day also no more exist. From this, however, the conclusion follows quite naturally that the entire globe itself once did not exist, and therefore will also one day exist no more in the future, because it consists of the sum of all earthly

Since, furthermore, all suns or solar stars are similar to our sun, their planets are also of the same nature as the planets of our sun. Consequently, all suns with their planets are transient: therefore, they once did not exist, and will one day no more exist.—So one concludes—but falsely.

The most excellent element of *fire* is called *combustible matter* or *phlogiston* <term>Phlogiston: An obsolete 18th-century chemical theory that hypothesized a fire-like element contained within combustible bodies that was released during combustion.</term>. When the smallest particles of a lump of matter, which contains a great deal of *combustible matter* in its mixture, are set into such great internal motion by some force that a dissolution or total separation thereof results: then such a lump of matter always exhibits that phenomenon which we call *fire*. For the effect of gravity is greater in the proximity of every celestial body than at a distance; consequently, it also compresses its atmosphere more densely nearby than further away. To this is added the weight with which the atmosphere compresses itself, which is the sum of the gravity of all its individual atoms taken together. Consequently, its steep cliffs cannot weather away, its mountains lose none of their height, they do not swell, and its volcanoes do not collapse, even though they have long since burnt out. Anyone who wishes to become intimately acquainted with its volcanic, wart-like face need only look it up in <term>Tobias Mayer’s</term> <note>Tobias Mayer (1723–1762) was a German astronomer famous for his highly accurate maps of the moon.</note> *unpublished works* <note>original: "operibus ineditis"</note>, where it is quite magnificently depicted. Furthermore, it does not rotate on its axis like the planets, but rather turns only once around itself during each of its periodic revolutions. Nor can it rotate in the same manner as the planets, because it was undoubtedly not balled together piece by piece above the Earth or in open space, but was ejected whole and all at once from the burning globe of the Earth.

In much the same way as our moon, the <term>moons of Saturn and Jupiter</term> likely appear, since they all possess little mass and, consequently, can have little air and few fluid materials similar to our water. But we now wish to cast another glance at the primary planets themselves.

Jupiter has a circumference forty times larger than our globe. Nevertheless, it rotates once on its axis within nine hours, whereas our globe requires twenty-four hours to complete one rotation. Therefore, Jupiter moves over a hundred times faster than our Earth. Because of this rotation, our own globe is even now gradually becoming thicker between the tropics, while sinking by the same amount near the poles. By virtue of the centrifugal force <note>original: "Dreheschwung"; literally "turning-swing," referring to the force generated by rotation.</note>, which is greatest between the tropics and smallest near the poles, the seawater rises from both poles toward the equator; the sea must then swell between the tropics and gradually flood the flat lands there, because not as much flows back as streams there from both sides. Since Jupiter now rotates a hundred times faster than the Earth, the centrifugal force near its equator must be a hundred times greater than that of our Earth at its equator. Consequently, Jupiter must swell far more at its equator than our globe; and astronomical measurements truly confirm that this planet is extraordinarily spheroidal or orange-shaped. It is, however, becoming even more spheroidal from time to time.

We will leave the planets now and turn to the comets.

These are not burning celestial bodies: for they shimmer with a far too pale glow, and do not shine like fire at all, but rather merely like **phosphorus**, whose dim light, as is known, only becomes visible in the dark, especially when it lies in a place where no vapors are present, such as in a vacuum. But in the daylight, or even in the presence of another light, one never notices its dull white shimmer, even if all moisture is removed from it. Namely, the rays of light from the sun seem to tear away large masses of them all around their edges and carry these away with them in straight lines. The brightest part of these is called the **nucleus**, which quite obviously consists of nothing but phosphorescent vapors, and only appears brighter because of its greater density than that which is found around and behind the nucleus. As the maws of the volcanoes were occasionally plugged for a short while with mountains of damp dust and ash from the aforementioned mighty cloudbursts, the atmosphere above them cooled down a little in the meantime. Water vapors gathered there in great quantities and now plunged down with all their might. These mountains, built up from volcanic ash clouds and watery vapors, which were still occasionally lifted up a little by the heat located beneath them, received from these swellings many fissures—both fine and coarse—which run down through them, sometimes vertically and sometimes obliquely. Dew and rain later seeped down into them and not only wonderfully dissolved their side walls, but also deposited metals or ores and crystals of all kinds, as well as other special types of minerals within them. In this same way, dew and rain still produce such minerals today in the clefts and fissures of the mountains, whenever they find materials therein that are suited for it. How this roughly happens can be gathered from the experiments of Mr. *Achard* <note>Franz Karl Achard (1753–1821), a chemist and physicist known for his research on the chemical constituents of precious stones.</note> regarding the components of gemstones. Mountain fissures that are empty are called empty clefts. If they are full of water, they are called water-clefts. However, in these conclusions, two fallacies <note>original: "Fallatien"; logical errors or deceptive arguments.</note> are clearly hidden.

The first fallacy consists in this: that one assumes the world to be merely the connection of the bodies and materials that exist in the world, and does not simultaneously take into account the **forces** <note>original: "Kräfte"; a central concept in 18th-century physics and metaphysics, referring to the underlying powers that cause physical phenomena.</note> that have formed these bodies and materials, and continue to form them. Materials are all sensible things, whether they have a certain shape or not. **Bodies**, on the other hand, are only those sensible things that have a specific shape. Water, wood, iron, earth, gold, etc., are thus mere materials; trees, houses, ducats, inkwells, etc., are bodies. — I only wanted to say this in passing — If one took proper account of the aforementioned forces, one could no longer conclude that they, too, are transitory or destructible, and consequently must have been created, even though materials and bodies are changeable and inconstant.

### 584 Thoughts on the Vocation

If I therefore assume God himself to be the **primal force** <note>German: *Urkraft*. A central concept in 18th-century German philosophy, referring to the fundamental energy from which all other forces derive.</note> of all beings, who created the world and still now directly works all changes in it, and still now directly forms all creatures: then I do nothing more than refrain from unnecessarily—and without having the slightest grounds for it—piling being upon being, merely to explain the existence of one from the existence of the other, since a single one is sufficient for it. 

But one must understand me correctly, and not imagine as if, according to this opinion, bodies and matter also belonged to God. These by no means belong to him because, as we have seen above, they are either mere **phenomena** <term>phenomena: things as they appear to our senses, as opposed to their true, underlying reality</term>, or at least possess no forces themselves essentially, but rather behave only passively, or merely allow the force to act upon them. If they seem to act back, they do not do it themselves, but rather only the force which shows itself active to us in them, but which for that reason does not belong to their essence. 

But if one nevertheless persists in the proposition that God and the aforementioned general world-force were distinct from one another, and if one considers my proposition—which is however already very old—to be daring: then let one tell me what God is doing at present, if he does not still constantly work, and consequently is not truly the cause of all changes, that is, the **force** of all effects that occur in the world, but rather lets everything proceed according to the laws which he formerly impressed upon nature?

---

### of Man by God. 585

In that case, would he not be of no more use to the world? Who is capable of thinking such a thing of God? How is it possible that a being, which is life, force, and activity itself, can be inactive?

That he should work only occasionally, and at another time not work, is also not easily conceivable, because in this case nothing in the world could occur according to definite laws and rules. One would have to expect every moment that God would hinder the course of nature now here, now elsewhere, and not let it occur according to the prescribed rules at all. From this, however, one would have to conclude that the rules themselves were not universally correct and applicable. From this, one would further have to conclude that God could not be infinitely wise and omniscient, because he had not adapted the laws right at the beginning to all occurrences that are supposed to be governed by them. Such a world would therefore unquestionably be a very imperfect thing, a mere **patchwork** <note>German: *Flickwerk*. Suggests something poorly made that requires constant repairs.</note>. But who can assert this with probability, unless he thoughtlessly imagines God like a human being, who indeed always finds much to mend in his works?

God thus works constantly. God is thus the cause of all effects that we perceive in the world. God works everything in—

### 586 Thoughts on the Vocation

...everything. **God is all in all.** <note>original: "Gott ist alles in allem." A reference to 1 Corinthians 15:28, a common proof-text in 18th-century philosophical theology.</note> These words are even the words of Scripture. If I therefore say: God is the **general force of nature**, which has formed everything and still forms everything, and also destroys everything again, then I am merely changing the name "God" into another—namely, into **general world-force**—but I agree perfectly with Scripture in this regard, considering the concept I attach to this expression.

Perhaps one imagines that in such a way, God is made the **author of evil**.

However, one must first consider that what is absolutely impossible cannot be made possible, much less real, even by God himself. The absolute best for every individual must therefore have been absolutely impossible in itself, if truly real evil exists in the world. Had everything in the world been intended to be absolutely good and perfect, then everything would have had to equal God himself in perfection and goodness. This, however, was absolutely impossible. If it had been possible, then God would have had to be able to create himself or other gods who were perfectly equal to him: and so he would no longer be the absolutely necessary highest being: thus he would not need to have his ground in himself, because other highest beings could have produced him.

<column-break/>

### 587 of Man through God

One sees clearly, therefore, what absurdities one falls into if one asserts the possibility of a world wherein all individuals are to be absolutely good and know nothing of any evil. Thus, for this reason alone, it follows that God or the **general world-force** must by no means be called the author of evil. This [evil] is absolutely necessary in every possible world because it is impossible for the creatures to be equal to the Creator, or the individual parts to be equal to the whole. But he is certainly the author of the good: for he has created everything, and still makes everything now, consequently also the good. Therefore, all good necessarily comes from him.

Many consider that to be an evil which others regard as the greatest luck? Certainly, there are also things that are considered evil by all people, e.g., sickness, hunger, poverty, and so forth. But whether these evils do not often bring about even more good when taken as a whole? If one goes back to the infinite goodness of God, one must indisputably...

Because I know nothing of it, remember nothing! I hear my opponents answer.

Man is therefore destined to elevate himself stepwise to higher perfections without ceasing, and thereby to make himself as happy as is ever possible—not his belly, but himself. His belly <note>The "belly" here represents physical appetites and purely biological needs.</note> is only destined to be perfect and good in its own way insofar as it must nourish and maintain the sense organs, without which man certainly cannot act properly in this life and cannot properly achieve his <term>vocation: the "Bestimmung" or ultimate purpose and destiny of a human being</term>. Here in this life, he lays the foundation for the future growth of his perfection and bliss. If he lays it on sand and builds upon it, the winds will blow his building over. He must build anew, lay the foundation anew. He always falls back as often as he wants to climb in such a way, and lets others, who are wiser, rise far above him. 

But the more firmly he grounds his foundation, the higher he elevates himself to the Creator through the use of his reason already in this life, the more he sharpens himself, and the more he seeks to become like God in his actions: to the greater perfections he ascends stepwise after this life, and to the more high bliss he attains after this life. God Himself, however, he certainly never equals, for He is infinitely perfect. He only approaches God infinitely, as the <term>hyperbola: a type of curve that continuously approaches a line without ever touching it</term> approaches its <term>asymptote: the straight line that the curve never reaches</term>, or as the <term>integrals: a mathematical method for calculating the area under a curve</term> of the differentials of the circle approach the true square-area <note>original: "Quadratinhalte"</note> of the circle. Whether he also acts upon matter after this life...

<summary>The author argues that human life is a process of "sharpening" the soul through reason to reach higher perfections, using mathematical metaphors to describe how humans infinitely approach God's perfection without ever reaching it.</summary>

Has God not moreover arranged the entire world so incomprehensibly beautiful, so good, so glorious, so wisely, for the sole purpose that all creatures may become as happy as is ever possible, and proceed from higher to higher <term>perfections</term> <note>The German "Vollkommenheiten" refers to the Enlightenment ideal of spiritual, intellectual, and moral growth.</note>? If man, along with his tools—I mean his sensory organs—were killed and made entirely inactive at once, he would undeniably be the most miserable creature on Earth, and God would have imprinted His image—I mean <term>reason</term>—upon him merely to make him all the more unhappy through it. The irrational animal knows no happiness but the life of its body, its fodder, and its reproductive instinct. Perhaps it does not even have actual knowledge of these things. Nevertheless, it flees death and hunger. Man, with his reason, raises himself infinitely above the cattle, and even dares to penetrate into the secrets of the Godhead, into the laws by which He governs the world. Yet should this being wish for perfection in vain? Should God have imprinted this holy wish so deeply upon him with fiery strokes in vain?

Growth in the knowledge of the truth, growth in the knowledge of God, is thus the <term>vocation of man</term> <note>original: "Bestimmung des Menschen." A central concept in 18th-century German Enlightenment philosophy, often referring to the ultimate purpose or destiny for which God created humanity.</note>, is eternal blessedness, is the natural and necessary consequence of his actions, of his deeds—the decay of the knowledge of the truth, the decay of the knowledge of God, is thus not the vocation of man, is wretchedness, and is likewise the natural and necessary consequence of his actions, of his deeds.

God, therefore, does not make the wise and good man happy merely because He wills it; rather, the wise and good man makes himself happy because his blessedness is the necessary and natural consequence of his actions—God, therefore, does not make the foolish and wicked man unhappy out of <term>caprice</term> <note>original: "Kaprize." Referring to an impulsive or arbitrary whim.</note>, like some stubborn despot, but the fool and the wicked man makes himself unhappy because his wretchedness—I mean the consciousness of his own decay, which he brings upon himself—is the necessary and natural consequence of his actions, of his deeds.

# Conclusion.

> Eternal, loving God, Father and Sustainer of the worlds! Hear my prayer! You know my heart! You know how often, how fervently, how urgently I have entreated You that You might lead me to the knowledge of the truth! You alone know what anxiety, what pains the doubts about the doctrines—which are held to be Your immediate will—have caused me! You alone know that I have never doubted out of frivolity, nor ever wished to examine and investigate generally prevailing opinions, passed down to us from antiquity and held to be Your Word, out of an inclination toward evil! Much that is passed off as Your own commands, as Your own words, I now recognize as **human work**, as fictions and fables. Holy, gracious Father! Forgive me if I err! Perhaps I am still in error! Should my book contain harmful errors, then grant that it may not be spread among my rational fellow creatures, but rather be buried in eternal oblivion: my wish is merely to fulfill Your will! My wish is to promote the happiness of my fellow creatures as much as possible! Should it, however, contain useful truth, then I know for certain in any case that You will provide for its distribution!
